Move the pen a short distance above the drawing area without pressing hard.
If it still fails, ask staff to test the connection.
why: Some tablets detect the pen before it touches the surface.

title: Tablet cursor moves but pen cannot draw
steps: Choose a brush in the approved drawing app.
Select a visible, editable layer and test a small mark in your own practice file.
If the mark never appears, ask the teacher.
why: A working pointer does not guarantee the current tool can paint.

title: Drawing tablet pen pressure not working
steps: Try light and medium strokes in an approved practice file.
Check whether the selected brush is intended to respond to pressure.
Ask your teacher to check tablet configuration if it does not. Do not install drivers.
why: Pressure response depends on the brush and tablet support.

title: Tablet pen draws before touching
steps: Lift the pen away from the surface and stop drawing.
Check visually whether the pen tip is stuck, without removing it.
Ask the teacher to inspect the pen.
why: A stuck tip or device fault can register contact unexpectedly.

title: Tablet pen cursor offset
steps: Test a small mark on a practice document.
Describe whether the offset happens everywhere or only near an edge.
Ask the teacher to check tablet mapping or calibration.
why: Calibration and mapping depend on the installed tablet model.

title: Drawing tablet covers wrong screen
steps: Identify the screen where the pointer appears.
Save your work if possible.
Ask the teacher to check the tablet's assigned display. Do not change mapping yourself.
why: A tablet can be mapped to another display.

title: Stylus tip is damaged
steps: Stop using the damaged pen on the tablet.
Show the teacher the tip without removing it.
Request an approved replacement pen or nib from staff.
why: A damaged nib can scratch a drawing surface.

title: Drawing tablet buttons do unexpected things
steps: Avoid pressing unknown tablet buttons.
Use the on-screen app tools instead.
Tell the teacher which button and action caused the problem.
why: Tablet buttons may be assigned custom shortcuts.

title: Drawing tablet is scratched or dirty
steps: Do not scrape the tablet or apply liquid.
Tell the teacher about the condition.
Use a different approved tablet if staff directs you.
why: Proper cleaning depends on the device material.

title: Stylus disappears when switching apps
aliases: tablet not working in photoshop only
steps: Test pen movement in the approved app where it works.
Open a small practice file in the intended app and choose an editable tool.
Tell the teacher which app fails. Do not change driver settings.
why: Different apps can handle pen input differently.

title: Wired game controller not detected
steps: Check the assigned controller's accessible USB connection.
Open the teacher-approved game's controller instructions or test screen.
If not recognized, ask the teacher. Do not install drivers.
why: Games differ in controller support.

title: Wireless controller does not connect
steps: Check the controller's ordinary power indicator.
Ask the teacher whether the controller is assigned to this station.
Let staff handle pairing or receiver changes.
why: Pairing can affect other classroom devices.

title: Controller buttons work in menus but not game
steps: Check that the approved game supports a controller for this activity.
Click or select the game's play area to give it focus.
Check the in-game controls help; ask the teacher if it still fails.
why: Menu and gameplay input may differ.

title: Controller joystick moves by itself
steps: Place the controller on a flat surface with sticks untouched.
See whether movement continues in the approved game.
Tell the teacher and request an approved spare. Do not open or calibrate it.
why: Unwanted movement may indicate stick drift.

title: Controller button sticks
steps: Stop pressing the damaged or sticky control.
Show the teacher which button is affected.
Do not pry the button or add cleaning liquid.
why: Physical cleaning and repair are staff tasks.

title: Game uses the wrong controller
steps: Pause the game if allowed.
Check the game's player assignment screen if available.
Ask the teacher to identify the correct assigned controller before changing connections.
why: Some games assign devices by connection order.

title: Controller works but game shows keyboard prompts
steps: Check the game's control reference screen.
Test a safe action in its practice mode.
If unsure which button matches the prompt, ask the teacher.
why: Some games display keyboard prompts even when controllers work.

title: Controller battery is low
steps: Pause and save if possible.
Tell the teacher the controller's battery indicator is low.
Use only the teacher-approved charger or spare.
why: Low battery can cause unexpected disconnections.

title: Wrong printer selected
steps: Open the approved app's print preview without submitting again.
Compare the selected printer name with the one assigned by your teacher.
Choose the assigned printer only if it is already available; otherwise ask staff.
why: School computers may list several shared printers.

title: Printer is missing from the list
steps: Open the normal Print dialog in the approved app.
Check the name your teacher provided.
If it is missing, cancel the dialog and ask staff. Do not add or install printers.
why: Printer availability is managed by school staff.

title: Printer says offline
steps: Cancel any repeated print attempts.
Note the assigned printer name and the exact message.
Ask your teacher to check the printer. Do not change its network or services.
why: Offline status may reflect a connection or device problem.

title: Print job is stuck
steps: Do not repeatedly submit the same document.
Note when you sent it and which printer was selected.
Ask the teacher to inspect the queue and cancel only your own job if needed.
why: Repeated submissions can waste paper once the queue resumes.

title: Accidentally sent too many copies
steps: Stop sending additional copies.
Tell your teacher immediately which document and printer were involved.
Ask staff to cancel the extra copies; do not cancel other students' jobs.
why: Shared queues can contain work from many students.

title: Print preview shows cut off edges
steps: Open Print Preview in the app.
Check the paper size and orientation required by your teacher.
If available, choose fit to page for your own print job and inspect the preview before printing.
why: The artwork may be larger than the printable area.

title: Print is sideways
steps: Open Print Preview.
Choose the teacher-required portrait or landscape option in the print dialog for your own job.
Check the preview before submitting once.
why: Print orientation affects how the page is placed on paper.

title: Only need to print one page
steps: Open the print dialog and identify the page number in the preview.
Choose the page-range control and enter just the required page, if supported.
Confirm the preview and copy count before printing.
why: A page range avoids unnecessary printing.

title: Printed page is black and white
steps: Check that the artwork itself has color in the app.
If the assigned print dialog offers color and your teacher permits it, select color for this job.
Ask the teacher if color is unavailable. Do not switch to another printer without permission.
why: Some school printers are monochrome or have managed color limits.

title: Printed page has streaks
steps: Keep the affected page to show the teacher.
Do not send the same job repeatedly.
Ask staff to inspect supplies or the printer.
why: Streaks may indicate a printer supply or mechanical issue.

title: Printer says paper jam
steps: Stop sending jobs.
Tell the teacher which printer reports a jam.
Do not reach inside, open hot areas or pull jammed paper yourself.
why: Printers can contain hot or moving components.

title: Printer says out of paper
steps: Stop sending repeat jobs.
Tell the teacher the printer name and message.
Wait for staff to refill the correct tray or direct you.
why: The printer may need a particular paper type or size.

title: Scanner cannot find device
steps: Use only the teacher-assigned scanner and approved scanning app.
Check that the assigned scanner appears in that app.
If not, ask the teacher. Do not install software or change network settings.
why: Scanners may be shared or require school-managed software.

title: Scanned document is upside down
steps: Inspect the preview in the approved scanning app.
Use its rotate control if available, or ask the teacher to show correct page placement.
Save to your assigned location only after checking readability.
why: Previewing helps catch orientation errors before saving.

title: Scanned file is missing
steps: Check the save location displayed by the approved scanning app.
Open that assigned folder and look for the file name you chose.
Tell the teacher if it is missing rather than repeatedly scanning confidential material.
why: Scanning creates a file in the selected destination.

title: Switch between open Windows apps
steps: Hold Alt and tap Tab until your approved app is selected.
Release Alt to return to that window.
Check that you are editing the correct document.
why: Alt + Tab switches among open windows.

title: Show all open Windows windows
steps: Press Windows + Tab.
Select your intended open window.
Press Esc if you opened the view by mistake.
why: Task View displays open windows.

title: Maximize a small window
steps: Click the square Maximize button near the top-right of your app.
If it is already maximized, the button may show overlapping squares.
Keep the work area visible and avoid the Close button beside it.
why: Maximizing increases the app's available workspace.

title: Put two windows side by side
steps: Open both approved apps.
Select one and press Windows + Left Arrow, then select the second app for the other side if prompted.
Restore the windows using their title bars when finished.
why: Snap arranges windows without changing system settings.

title: Window is off the edge of the screen
steps: Select the approved app on the taskbar.
Try Windows + Up Arrow to maximize the active window.
If it is still missing, ask the teacher rather than changing display configuration.
why: Maximizing can restore a window to the visible work area.

title: Desktop icons disappeared behind windows
steps: Press Windows + D to reveal the desktop.
Press the same shortcut again to return to your windows.
Check that your open project is still present.
why: Showing the desktop hides windows temporarily, not their files.

title: Windows app will not open
steps: Try opening the assigned app once from its usual shortcut.
Wait briefly for it to load; do not repeatedly click.
If there is an error, show the teacher. Do not download or reinstall the app.
why: An app may take time to start or need staff repair.

title: Program opens multiple copies
steps: Use Alt + Tab to identify each open window.
Save work in the correct document.
Close only extra windows you opened and do not need, checking any save prompt.
why: Repeated launch clicks may create extra windows.

title: App asks to save when closing
steps: Read the document name in the prompt.
Choose Save if you want to keep your changes, or Cancel if unsure.
If the original belongs to someone else, ask the teacher before overwriting it.
why: Save prompts protect unsaved work.

title: App asks to update
steps: Save your current work if the app permits.
Do not approve installation or enter administrator credentials.
Show the teacher the update message.
why: School IT manages application updates.

title: Windows sign-in screen is locked
steps: Check that this is your assigned classroom computer.
Use only your own school-approved sign-in method.
If it shows another user's session or your account fails, ask your teacher.
why: Shared computers require authorized accounts.

title: Computer says restart required
steps: Save your work in the assigned location if possible.
Tell the teacher the exact restart message.
Do not restart shared computers unless directed.
why: A restart can close work and interrupt classroom activity.

title: Windows computer has no power
steps: Check for visible power indicators on the assigned computer and monitor.
If the teacher normally permits powering on your station, use its ordinary power button once.
If there is no response, ask staff. Do not inspect power strips or rear cables.
why: The monitor and computer have separate power states.

title: Computer is running very slowly
steps: Save your own current work.
Close approved apps or tabs you no longer need using their normal Close controls.
If it remains slow, ask the teacher. Do not use system cleanup or task-management tools.
why: Several open apps can compete for resources.

title: App window is blank white
steps: Wait a short time for the app to load.
If controls respond, save work before switching to another window.
If still blank, ask the teacher to assess it before closing.
why: An app may be busy or have a display problem.

title: Windows asks for administrator permission
steps: Do not approve the prompt or enter credentials.
Cancel if the normal Cancel or No button is available.
Tell your teacher what action opened it.
why: Protected actions require authorized staff.

title: Windows reports low disk space
steps: Save your current work to the approved school location if possible.
Tell your teacher about the storage warning.
Do not delete system files, other students' work or use cleanup utilities.
why: Staff can manage shared storage safely.

title: File Explorer open assigned folder
steps: Press Windows + E or use the File Explorer taskbar icon.
Open the teacher-assigned folder from the navigation list.
If the shared folder is unavailable, ask the teacher rather than browsing other users' folders.
why: File Explorer is for accessing authorized files and folders.

title: Find Downloads folder on Windows
steps: Open File Explorer.
Choose Downloads if it appears in the navigation pane.
Look for your own file by name or recent date; ask the teacher if downloads use another folder.
why: Browser downloads often go to a designated folder.

title: Rename your own Windows file
steps: Select your own file in File Explorer.
Use the normal Rename option from the context menu.
Enter the required name, preserving the existing file type if shown.
why: Renaming a file does not convert it to another format.

title: Create a folder for class work
steps: Open your assigned storage location in File Explorer.
Use New > Folder or the available New folder control.
Give it the class or project name required by your teacher.
why: Folders help keep project files together.

title: Copy your own file to another folder
steps: Select your own file in File Explorer and press Ctrl + C.
Open the teacher-approved destination folder.
Press Ctrl + V and confirm the copied file opens. Leave the original in place.
why: Copying creates another file without moving the original.

title: File is already open and cannot be moved
steps: Save and close your own file from the app using it.
Try moving it only if your teacher has approved the destination.
If the message continues, ask staff; do not force-close processes.
why: Open files can be locked to prevent conflicting changes.

title: File opens in wrong program
steps: Open the teacher-approved app first.
Use File > Open to select your own project file.
Do not change Windows default apps. Ask the teacher if the file still fails.
why: Opening files from within an app avoids changing system defaults.

title: Windows file says access denied
steps: Check that the file is in your assigned school folder.
Do not try another account or change permissions.
Show the teacher the location and message.
why: Access restrictions protect other people and school resources.

title: Screenshot copied but not saved
steps: Open the capture notification if it is still visible.
Use Save in Snipping Tool if available and select the assigned location.
If the capture is only on the clipboard, paste into the teacher-approved app or take another permitted screenshot.
why: A screenshot can be copied without becoming a file.

title: Capture just part of the Windows screen
steps: Press Windows + Shift + S.
Choose rectangular capture if available and drag around your own work only.
Open the capture notification to save, or paste into the assigned document. Avoid capturing private information.
why: A selected region is useful for process screenshots.

title: Cancel a screenshot in Windows
steps: Press Esc before selecting an area.
Check that your original app is active again.
If the screen stays dim, ask the teacher.
why: Esc normally cancels an unfinished capture.

title: Paste a screenshot into an assignment
steps: Take a permitted screenshot of your own work.
Click the intended place in the approved document or slide.
Press Ctrl + V if the screenshot is on the clipboard, then adjust size as needed.
why: The clipboard can transfer images between supported apps.

title: Windows taskbar is hidden
steps: Move the pointer to the bottom edge of the screen.
If the taskbar appears, choose the assigned app.
If it remains hidden, ask the teacher. Do not change taskbar settings.
why: The taskbar may be temporarily hidden or covered by an app.

title: Find an approved installed app
steps: Open Start and type the name of the teacher-approved installed app.
Select the matching app only if it is already available.
If it is not listed, ask your teacher. Do not install it from a web result.
why: Start search can locate installed applications.

title: Classroom class is missing
steps: Open the Classes page and check that the class name matches your schedule.
Check the account icon for your assigned school account, without signing out of a shared computer.
If the class is absent, ask your teacher to check enrollment.
why: Only enrolled classes appear for your account.

title: Find assignments by topic
steps: Open your class and select Classwork.
Look for the topic or unit named by your teacher.
Open the assignment title to see its directions.
why: Classwork is organized separately from Stream posts.

title: Classroom Stream versus Classwork
steps: Use Stream for class announcements and recent posts.
Use Classwork to locate the actual assignment and its attachments.
why: The two tabs have different purposes.

title: Find due dates in Classroom
steps: Open the assignment from Classwork.
Look near its title for the due date and time, if one is set.
Ask your teacher if the due date is absent or confusing.
why: Not every item has a due date.

title: Find your Classroom to-do list
steps: Open Classroom and look for the To-do page in its navigation, if available.
Filter by class or look for your assigned, missing or done work.
Open the exact item before deciding what to do.
why: The overview helps you find work, but teachers can update statuses.

title: Find all your work for one class
steps: Open the class and go to Classwork.
Look for View your work if available, or use the class's work overview.
Check the status and due date for each item.
why: The class-specific view helps separate assignments from different classes.

title: Classroom material has no Turn in button
steps: Check whether the item is labeled Material rather than Assignment.
Read the directions and locate the assignment your teacher actually wants submitted.
Ask if there is no separate submission item.
why: Materials may be reference documents rather than assignments.

title: Find a linked tutorial in Classroom
steps: Open the assignment details.
Look below the instructions for links, videos or file attachments.
Open only the resource your teacher identifies; report broken links.
why: Resource attachments are separate from your submitted work.

title: Classroom instructions are cut off
steps: Open the full assignment rather than the preview on Classwork.
Scroll through the instructions and expand text if the option is shown.
Open attached rubrics or direction documents if your teacher included them.
why: The full assignment may contain more directions than the overview.

title: Classroom assignment is locked or unavailable
steps: Check that the correct class and school account are open.
Read any displayed message without trying to bypass it.
Ask the teacher whether access or scheduling needs attention.
why: The teacher controls assignment availability.

title: Classroom calendar for assignments
steps: Look for the calendar in Classroom navigation or the Classwork page.
Choose the appropriate class or week.
Open an item to confirm its actual instructions in Classroom.
why: Calendar entries are a reminder, not a substitute for assignment directions.

title: Classroom class code does not work
steps: Make sure the code came directly from your teacher and matches the class.
Check for typing mistakes, spaces and similar-looking letters or numbers.
Ask the teacher for an updated invitation if it still fails.
why: Class codes may expire or be disabled.

title: Open your assigned copy of a document
aliases: teacher made copy for each student
steps: Open the assignment and look at Your work.
Open the document assigned to you, not the original resource in the instructions.
Check that your own copy is editable before starting.
why: A teacher may provide a separate editable copy for every student.

title: Classroom document says view only
steps: Open the document from Your work instead of the class resource link.
If already turned in, ask whether corrections are allowed before unsubmit.
If it remains view only, let the teacher check access.
why: The original resource or submitted copy may not be editable.

title: Classroom Mark as done versus Turn in
steps: Read the instructions to see whether a file is required.
Complete the required work; attach it if the teacher requires a file.
Use the completion button shown and confirm the status changes.
why: Assignments without attached student work may use a different completion label.

title: Classroom upload stuck in progress
steps: Keep the assignment open and wait for the attachment to finish.
Check that you still have the original saved file and permitted internet connection.
If upload never finishes, ask your teacher before trying again.
why: An unfinished upload may not become part of the submission.

title: Classroom submit a downloaded image
steps: Find the exported PNG or JPG in Files or File Explorer.
In the assignment, use Add or create and choose File if available.
Select the correct image, wait for upload, then complete submission as directed.
why: Exporting an image does not automatically attach it to Classroom.

title: Classroom attach a Google Drive document
steps: Open Your work and choose the Drive option under Add or create.
Pick your own finished document and confirm it appears in Your work.
Turn in only after checking the correct attachment.
why: The Drive picker links the chosen file to the assignment.

title: Classroom submit more than one file
steps: Add each required file from Your work using the appropriate file or Drive picker.
Wait until both appear and verify their names.
Turn in the assignment once all required attachments are present.
why: A project may require both editable work and an exported image.

title: Classroom wrong file attached before submitting
steps: In Your work, identify the mistaken attachment by opening or checking its name.
Use the remove option for that attachment if available; keep the original file saved.
Add the correct file and verify it before turning in.
why: Removing an attachment is not the same as deleting its original file.

title: Classroom accidentally submitted too early
steps: Check whether the assignment status is Turned in.
Ask your teacher if you may unsubmit or make corrections; follow classroom rules.
If allowed, complete the correction and resubmit before the required deadline.
why: Unsubmitting changes the submission status and may affect deadlines.

title: Classroom submission status is still assigned
steps: Open the assignment and inspect Your work status.
Check whether the required attachments are uploaded and the completion button was confirmed.
Tell your teacher if status does not update; keep your saved work.
why: Uploading a file alone may not complete submission.

title: Classroom late or missing label
steps: Check the displayed due date and current submission status.
Open Your work and verify you attached the intended files.
Contact your teacher if the label seems incorrect; do not submit duplicate copies unless asked.
why: A missing or late label does not always mean a file was lost.

title: Classroom returned work is editable again
steps: Open the returned assignment and read teacher feedback.
Check whether corrections are allowed under your class rules.
If permitted, edit your own copy and resubmit as directed.
why: Returned work may allow editing without granting permission for unlimited corrections.

title: Classroom cannot open attachment preview
steps: Check the file name and whether it is an expected format.
Use the normal open option for the assigned file if available.
Report the exact error to your teacher rather than installing a viewer.
why: Some file types or permissions prevent previewing.

title: Classroom submission includes old version
steps: Compare the attachment name and preview with your latest saved file.
If already submitted, ask permission before changing the submission.
If the teacher allows it, attach the required final version and resubmit.
why: A downloaded file and a live Drive document update differently.

title: Classroom upload file too large
steps: Keep the original project saved.
Check the file type and size against the assignment instructions.
Ask the teacher whether a smaller approved export is acceptable.
why: Reducing size can affect image quality or remove editable features.

title: Find private comments in Classroom
steps: Open the exact assignment.
Find the private comments area in the assignment details, if available.
Read the message and only reply with school-related information.
why: Private assignment comments are distinct from class-wide posts.

title: Find comments inside a Google document
steps: Open the attached document from the returned assignment.
Look for comment bubbles beside the affected content or the comments panel.
Read each comment alongside the selected passage; ask before resolving feedback.
why: In-document comments may not appear in the main Classroom comment area.

title: Find a Classroom rubric
steps: Open the assignment and look for its rubric in the details.
Expand the criteria or scoring levels if shown.
Ask the teacher for clarification if no rubric is attached.
why: A rubric may be attached only to certain assignments.

title: Classroom grade does not appear
steps: Open the assignment and check its return status.
Look for a score or feedback in the completed work area.
Ask the teacher when grades will be posted; do not try to access gradebook tools.
why: Teachers decide when grades are returned.

title: Classroom grade is different from expected
steps: Check the assignment name, score and maximum points.
Read the teacher feedback and rubric.
Ask your teacher about any discrepancy respectfully.
why: Only the teacher can correct grading records.

title: Classroom reply to teacher feedback
steps: Open the assignment feedback area.
If allowed by your teacher, enter your own brief explanation of what you changed.
Review it and use the private comment send button.
why: TechGuide can show where to reply, not write your response.

title: Classroom comment box is missing
steps: Check whether you are on the assignment details rather than the class Stream.
Look for private comments or a document comment area.
If commenting is unavailable, use the teacher-approved communication method.
why: Teachers and school policies may restrict comments.

title: Classroom announcement disappears
steps: Check the correct class and Stream page.
Look in Classwork for related instructions or materials.
Ask the teacher whether the announcement was moved or removed.
why: Stream posts can be updated by the teacher.

title: Classroom notification opens wrong class
steps: Open Classroom directly from your usual school bookmark.
Choose the correct class and assignment title.
Ask your teacher if the notification no longer matches an available item.
why: Old notification links may not reflect updated assignments.

title: Classroom cannot see classmate work
steps: Only open items your teacher explicitly shared with you.
Do not attempt to access other students' submissions or private feedback.
Ask the teacher where to find the class-approved example.
why: Student submissions and grades are private.

title: Find recently opened Google Drive files
steps: Open Google Drive and look for Recent.
Check the title and owner of the file you recognize.
Open your own or teacher-shared file.
why: Recent is a view of files, not their actual storage folder.

title: Find files shared by a teacher
steps: Open Drive and choose Shared with me.
Search for the file title or the teacher's name using available filters.
If it is missing, ask the teacher to confirm sharing.
why: Shared files may not appear in My Drive.

title: Search Drive by file type
steps: Use the Drive search box.
Choose the available Type filter, such as PDF or image.
Confirm the name and owner before opening a result.
why: Filtering helps narrow a long search list.

title: Search Drive by modified date
steps: Open Drive search filters.
Choose a Last modified date or range if offered.
Check the titles and preview your own work.
why: Modified dates can be different from creation dates.

title: Create a class folder in Google Drive
steps: Open your own approved My Drive location.
Choose New and Folder.
Name it for your class or project and open the folder to confirm.
why: Folders organize files without changing their format.

title: Move your own Google Drive file into a folder
steps: Select your own file in Drive.
Use the Organize or Move option if available.
Choose your own class folder and confirm the move; do not move shared originals.
why: Moving a file changes its location and can affect access in shared folders.

title: Star an important Drive file
steps: Select your own or authorized shared file.
Use the Organize menu or Add to starred option.
Find it later in Starred.
why: A star is a personal shortcut and does not move the original.

title: Remove a personal Drive star
steps: Open Starred in Drive.
Identify the intended file and use Remove from starred.
Check that it is still available in its original folder.
why: Unstarring is not deleting the file.

title: Find where a Drive file is stored
aliases: which folder is my doc in
steps: Select the known file in Drive.
Use File information or file details to inspect its location if shown.
Open the parent folder only if you are authorized.
why: A search result can come from different folders.

title: Drive grid versus list view
steps: Open your Drive file list.
Use the layout toggle if visible to switch between thumbnails and a list.
Choose whichever view helps you identify your own file.
why: List view makes names easier to compare.

title: Sort your Drive files by name
steps: Open your own Drive folder.
In list view, use the Name column or sort menu.
Check whether sort is ascending or descending.
why: Sorting changes the view, not the files themselves.

title: Drive shortcut versus actual file
steps: Look for a shortcut arrow on the file icon.
Open the shortcut to reach the intended authorized file.
If its target is unavailable, ask the owner; do not create new permissions.
why: A shortcut points to another item rather than copying its contents.

title: Find a file in Drive Trash
steps: Open Trash in your own Drive.
Locate only the file you accidentally removed.
If it is yours and the Restore option is available, restore it; ask staff about shared files.
why: Restoration may return a file to its former location; do not empty Trash.

title: Drive duplicate files with similar names
steps: Compare the filename, owner and modified time in Drive.
Open your own likely copies and inspect their contents.
Ask your teacher which to submit; do not delete other copies until confirmed.
why: Copies are independent files and may contain different edits.

title: Drive file has an untitled name
steps: Search for Untitled and use a recent date or file-type filter.
Preview only your own likely files.
Rename the correct file using your teacher's naming convention.
why: A meaningful name helps prevent accidental submissions.

title: Drive folder appears empty
steps: Check the account and exact folder path.
Search for one expected filename in Drive.
If the folder was shared, ask its owner to check access rather than changing it yourself.
why: An empty view may be a different folder or restricted access.

title: Upload a local file to Google Drive
steps: Open your own school Drive folder.
Choose New and File upload.
Select your saved file, wait for completion and check that it opens.
why: Uploading creates a Drive copy; your local original remains separate.

title: Download an approved Google Drive file
steps: Select the file provided by your teacher or owned by you.
Use Download if available and allowed.
Check the Downloads location for the expected name.
why: Drive downloads may be disabled by the owner or school.

title: Drive download contains several files in a ZIP
steps: Locate the downloaded ZIP file.
Use the normal built-in extraction feature on the computer if permitted.
Open the extracted folder and verify the individual files.
why: A ZIP packages several files together without changing their contents.

title: Drive upload failed or interrupted
steps: Keep the source file saved and check the permitted connection.
Read the upload error and ensure the file is not still uploading.
Tell your teacher if it fails again; avoid repeatedly uploading duplicates.
why: An interrupted transfer may not create a usable copy.

title: Drive says you are offline
steps: Check whether the school-approved network is connected.
Keep your document open if edits are not yet saved.
Ask your teacher if the connection does not return; do not change network settings.
why: Offline access depends on school policy and whether a file was prepared for offline use.

title: Google Docs changes have not saved to Drive
steps: Keep the editing tab open.
Look at the save or connection status near the document title.
If allowed, preserve your work through the teacher-approved method and report the warning.
why: Unsynced changes may be lost if the page closes unexpectedly.

title: Drive file shared link opens wrong account
steps: Check the account shown in the upper corner.
Use your existing assigned school account if your teacher permits switching accounts.
If there is no authorized account available, ask the teacher.
why: Access is tied to the account the owner shared with.

title: Request access to a teacher file
steps: Verify that you are using your assigned school account and correct link.
If Request access is offered and the teacher directs you to use it, send the request to the file owner.
Wait for the teacher to approve; do not try alternate accounts or permission workarounds.
why: Only the file owner or authorized staff can grant access.

title: Understand viewer, commenter and editor access
steps: Look at the access mode shown in the document.
Viewer can read, commenter can leave feedback when allowed, and editor can change content.
Ask the owner if your authorized role is incorrect.
why: Access levels protect shared work from unintended changes.

title: Drive says storage quota exceeded
steps: Save your active work without deleting anything important.
Read the quota warning and ask your teacher or IT for an approved storage option.
Do not empty Trash, remove shared items or create another account to avoid limits.
why: School storage limits are managed by staff.

title: Google file not owned by you
steps: Check the displayed owner in Drive file details.
Use the shared file only as the teacher instructs.
Ask for your own copy if editing is required.
why: Shared ownership and editing access are different things.

title: Find file size in Google Drive
steps: Select the uploaded file and inspect file details or the size column if present.
Compare its size with the teacher's upload requirement.
If it is too large, ask about an approved export format.
why: Native Google documents may not show a conventional file size.

title: Drive PDF preview appears blank
steps: Wait briefly for the preview to render.
Try the normal open option if allowed, checking the file is the correct one.
Ask the teacher if the PDF still appears blank; do not download unknown viewers.
why: Blank previews can result from a damaged file or a rendering problem.

title: Drive file is a shortcut with access denied
steps: Check that the link points to the teacher-assigned file.
Use your school account and open it normally.
Ask the owner to check the original target's access.
why: A shortcut does not give permission to open its target.

title: Editable project versus exported image
steps: Check which file type your teacher requests.
Keep the editable PSD or AI project with layers or vectors.
Save a separate PNG or JPG export if requested and attach both only as directed.
why: An image export is not a substitute for editable source work.

title: PNG versus JPG
steps: Use PNG if transparency or lossless image storage is required.
Use JPG if your teacher requests a photo-style compressed file without transparency.
Check the assignment before exporting.
why: JPEG compression can reduce detail and does not support transparent backgrounds.

title: PDF versus Google document
steps: Check whether your teacher asks for an editable document or a PDF.
Keep the original Google Doc and download a separate PDF using its File menu if required.
Preview the PDF before submitting.
why: A PDF preserves layout but is not the same as the editable source.

title: SVG versus PNG
steps: Check whether the task requests a vector file or a raster image.
Use the Adobe app's approved export format for the requested output.
Keep the source project and preview the export.
why: SVG can store scalable vectors; PNG stores pixels.

title: File extension seems wrong
steps: Look at the existing file type rather than just its displayed name.
Open the original in the appropriate classroom application.
Use Save As or Export to make the required format; do not just rename its extension.
why: Renaming an extension does not convert the file.

title: File opens in wrong application
steps: Check the original file type and intended classroom software.
Open that application and use File > Open to select your file.
If the app is not available, ask your teacher rather than changing system defaults.
why: Opening from the intended program avoids modifying system settings.

title: Downloaded file name ends with (1)
steps: Find the original and numbered copy in your Downloads folder.
Compare name, date and preview to identify the final version.
Rename or move only your own correct copy according to directions.
why: Browsers often add a number to avoid overwriting a file.

title: A file is too large for the assignment
steps: Keep your editable original and check the requested file format.
Use the assigned application's export options only if your teacher approves smaller dimensions or compression.
Preview the result to make sure it remains legible.
why: Compression or resizing can remove details, so keep the original.

title: Cannot find a saved Adobe project on Chromebook
aliases: adobe file from windows not on chromebook
steps: Check where the project was saved on the Windows computer.
Use only the teacher-approved Drive or shared location for transferring your own saved file.
If it was saved locally, ask your teacher how to retrieve it.
why: Local files do not automatically appear on another computer.

title: Cloud copy versus computer copy
aliases: why file different on another computer
steps: Check whether the current file is in Drive or in local Downloads/Documents.
Compare the latest modification date and open your own copies to confirm.
Use your teacher's approved storage location for the version you need.
why: A local copy may not sync when a cloud file changes.

title: Check an exported image before turning it in
steps: Find the exported file in the folder selected during export.
Open it using the normal image viewer or preview.
Check the edges, orientation, readability and required filename before attaching.
why: An export may look different from an editable project.

title: Keep source and export together
steps: Make or open your own assigned project folder.
Save the source file and the requested export using clear matching names.
Check both files are present before leaving the computer.
why: A consistent folder makes it easier to find the correct version later.

title: Avoid accidentally overwriting your project
steps: Read the replacement warning carefully.
If you are unsure, cancel and keep both versions with clear names if allowed.
Verify which is the final version before submitting.
why: Replacing a file can remove an earlier version.

title: Google Docs rename a document
steps: Click your own document title at the top.
Type the required filename and press Enter.
Check the title after saving.
why: The document title helps you locate it in Drive.

title: Google Docs undo accidental typing
steps: Press Ctrl + Z or use the Undo toolbar button immediately.
Check that only the intended change was reversed.
If older content is missing, ask the teacher before restoring a version.
why: Undo reverses recent editing actions.

title: Google Docs redo a change
steps: Use the Redo toolbar button after undoing.
Check the restored text and formatting.
why: Redo reapplies an action you just reversed.

title: Google Docs select all text
steps: Click inside the document body.
Press Ctrl + A, then verify the intended text is selected before formatting.
Click away to cancel selection if needed.
why: Selecting broad content can affect the entire document.

title: Google Docs paste without formatting
steps: Copy your own approved text.
Place the cursor in your document and press Ctrl + Shift + V if available.
Check its appearance and use your required formatting.
why: Plain-text paste avoids bringing in the original font and color.

title: Google Docs text is tiny
steps: Select the affected text.
Use the font-size control in the toolbar and choose the required size.
Check the document zoom if the entire page looks tiny.
why: Font size changes the document; zoom changes your view.

title: Google Docs change text color
steps: Select the text you want to format.
Open the Text color button in the toolbar and choose the required color.
Check that the text remains easy to read.
why: Text color is different from the background highlight.

title: Google Docs remove text highlight
steps: Select the highlighted text.
Use the Highlight color control and choose None if available.
Check whether the color was actually text shading or a table cell background.
why: Highlight is a separate format from font color.

title: Google Docs bold, italic and underline
steps: Select the words that need formatting.
Use B, I or U in the toolbar as required.
Click elsewhere to check the result.
why: Formatting applies to the selected words or future typing at the cursor.

title: Google Docs remove unwanted formatting
steps: Select the affected text only.
Choose Format > Clear formatting if available.
Reapply the teacher-required formatting as needed.
why: Clearing formatting changes styles, not the text itself.

title: Google Docs center a heading
steps: Place the cursor in the heading paragraph.
Use the alignment control and choose Center.
Check that only the intended paragraph changed.
why: Paragraph alignment is not controlled by extra spaces.

title: Google Docs line spacing
steps: Select the paragraphs you need to format.
Open Format > Line & paragraph spacing or its toolbar control.
Choose the spacing requested by your teacher.
why: Line spacing controls vertical distance between lines.

title: Google Docs extra space between paragraphs
steps: Click near the extra gap and check whether blank paragraphs exist.
Use the line and paragraph spacing menu to inspect spacing before or after paragraphs.
Adjust only according to the assignment instructions.
why: Blank lines and paragraph spacing create gaps differently.

title: Google Docs indent a paragraph
steps: Place the cursor in the paragraph.
Use Format > Align & indent > Indentation options if available.
Set the teacher-requested first-line or paragraph indent.
why: Indentation formats paragraphs more consistently than repeated spaces.

title: Google Docs make a bulleted list
steps: Select your own list text or place the cursor where the list begins.
Use the Bulleted list toolbar button.
Press Enter to add another item and Enter again on an empty item to end the list.
why: List formatting keeps the bullets aligned.

title: Google Docs make a numbered list
steps: Select your own items or place the cursor at the starting point.
Choose the Numbered list toolbar option.
Enter each item on its own line and stop the list when finished.
why: Automatic numbering follows the list structure.

title: Google Docs numbering restarts incorrectly
steps: Click the number in your own list.
Use the list context menu to continue previous numbering or restart if offered.
Review the sequence afterward.
why: Separate list sections may use independent numbering.

title: Google Docs heading styles
steps: Select a heading you already wrote.
Use the paragraph styles dropdown and select the appropriate heading level.
Check the document outline if shown.
why: Heading styles identify structure for navigation and accessibility.

title: Google Docs find a word
steps: Press Ctrl + F inside the document.
Type the word or phrase you are looking for.
Use the results to navigate, then close the search box.
why: Find does not alter document text.

title: Google Docs replace a repeated typo
steps: Use Edit > Find and replace if available.
Enter the old and corrected text.
Review each match and replace only the intended occurrences.
why: Replacing all without reviewing may change unintended words.

title: Google Docs spelling underlines
steps: Read the underlined word and check it against your own intended spelling.
Click or right-click to see any suggestions if available.
Choose a suggestion only if it fits your meaning.
why: Spelling checks are suggestions, not proof that a word is wrong.

title: Google Docs word count
steps: Use Tools > Word count if available.
If you want the count of one section, select it first.
Read the count and compare with your teacher's directions.
why: Word count can apply to the document or selected text.

title: Google Docs insert a link
steps: Select your own text or place the cursor at the intended link location.
Use Insert > Link or Ctrl + K.
Paste only the teacher-approved URL and check the displayed text before applying.
why: A hyperlink can have a readable label separate from its address.

title: Google Docs insert a table
steps: Place the cursor where the table belongs.
Choose Insert > Table and select the needed rows and columns.
Enter your own assignment information in the cells.
why: A table organizes data into rows and columns.

title: Google Docs add a table row
steps: Click a cell in your own table.
Use its context menu to insert a row above or below.
Check that your information remains correctly aligned.
why: A table row is different from a text line.

title: Google Docs table column too narrow
steps: Click inside the table.
Drag the intended column boundary or use Table properties if available.
Ensure all columns still fit on the page.
why: Wider columns reduce wrapping but use more page width.

title: Google Docs merge table cells
steps: Select the adjacent cells in your own table.
Use the table context menu to choose Merge cells if offered.
Check that no important text was lost or moved unexpectedly.
why: Merging changes the table layout.

title: Google Docs image moves text around
steps: Click the image and inspect the layout options beneath it.
Choose In line or the wrapping arrangement required by your teacher.
Check the nearby paragraph and the next page.
why: Image positioning affects text flow.

title: Google Docs resize an image without stretching
steps: Select your own inserted image.
Drag a corner handle rather than a side if preserving proportions.
Compare the result to the original and undo if stretched.
why: Corner resizing generally preserves proportions in Docs.

title: Google Docs image crop
steps: Select the inserted image.
Use the Crop image control if available and adjust the crop handles.
Confirm the crop and verify the visible area.
why: Cropping hides the unwanted edges instead of stretching the image.

title: Google Docs add alt text to image
steps: Select the image.
Use the image context menu or Image options to find Alt text if available.
Write your own short description of what the image communicates.
why: Alt text helps people who cannot see the image.

title: Google Docs page margins
steps: If the document uses pages, open File > Page setup.
Check the margins and units required by your teacher.
Apply only the requested document layout changes.
why: Margins control printable space, not system settings.

title: Google Docs landscape page
steps: In a paged document, open File > Page setup.
Choose Landscape if the assignment requires it.
Review the layout after applying.
why: Orientation changes the document page, not your monitor.

title: Google Docs page numbers missing
steps: In a document using pages, open Insert and look for the page number option.
Select the location or numbering style required by the assignment.
Check the first and following pages.
why: Page numbers are usually placed in headers or footers.

title: Google Docs header or footer
steps: In a paged document, open Insert and find Headers and footers, or double-click the existing header/footer area.
Add your own required information.
Click back into the body to continue editing.
why: Headers and footers occupy separate areas from body text.

title: Google Docs no page boundaries
steps: Look at File > Page setup to determine if the document is pageless.
If your teacher requires printable pages, choose Pages and confirm the document layout.
Do not change the browser or computer display settings.
why: Pageless layout does not use conventional page breaks.

title: Google Docs blank page at end
steps: Click near the end and check for extra blank lines or a page break.
Remove only the unnecessary blank paragraph or break with Backspace if safe.
Check that the actual assignment content remains.
why: Extra paragraphs and breaks can create empty pages.

title: Google Docs print preview
steps: Open File > Print or the print toolbar button.
Inspect the preview for page count, clipped text and blank pages.
Cancel unless your teacher has approved printing.
why: Preview helps avoid wasted paper.

title: Google Docs download as PDF
steps: With your own document open, use File > Download > PDF Document if provided.
Find the downloaded PDF and preview it.
Keep your original editable document.
why: The PDF is a separate exported copy.

title: Google Docs view version history
steps: In your own editable file, use File > Version history > See version history if available.
Inspect the earlier versions without restoring them.
Ask the teacher before restoring any work, especially if shared.
why: Restoration can replace newer work; viewing history is safer.

title: Google Docs suggestion mode is on
steps: Check the editing-mode dropdown near the toolbar.
If your teacher permits editing your own document and Editing is available, choose it.
If the mode is restricted, ask the owner.
why: Suggesting tracks proposals instead of directly changing content.

title: Google Docs menu or toolbar missing
steps: Check whether you are in the document body or a preview.
Look for the menu visibility arrow or leave browser full-screen mode with the normal key if needed.
Ask if your access is view only.
why: A compact view or limited access can hide editing controls.

title: Google Slides add a new slide
steps: Open your own presentation.
Click the plus button or use Slide > New slide.
Choose a suitable layout through Layout if needed.
why: Each slide is a separate page in a presentation.

title: Google Slides duplicate a slide
steps: Select the slide thumbnail on the left.
Use its context menu and choose Duplicate slide.
Edit the copy rather than accidentally replacing the original.
why: Duplicating preserves the existing arrangement and objects.

title: Google Slides reorder slides
steps: Select a slide thumbnail in the left sidebar.
Drag it between the intended thumbnails.
Review the slide order from top to bottom.
why: Reordering thumbnails changes presentation sequence.

title: Google Slides delete an accidental blank slide
steps: Select the unintended blank slide thumbnail.
Verify it does not contain required work and use Delete.
Use Undo immediately if the wrong slide disappears.
why: Deleting a slide removes all objects on that slide.

title: Google Slides slide layout
steps: Select the slide thumbnail.
Use the Layout control or Slide menu.
Choose the required arrangement and check your existing content.
why: Layouts supply placeholders for titles and content.

title: Google Slides change theme
steps: Open your own presentation and locate Theme in the toolbar or Slide menu.
Preview available themes.
Apply only one suitable for the assignment and review all slides.
why: Themes may change colors, fonts and placeholders throughout the deck.

title: Google Slides slide background
steps: Select the intended slide.
Use Slide > Change background or the Background button.
Choose the required color or approved image and confirm.
why: A background differs from a shape placed over a slide.

title: Google Slides page size
steps: Open File > Page setup.
Check the page size or aspect ratio requested by your teacher.
Preview all slides after changing it, since objects may move.
why: Page setup changes the dimensions of the entire presentation.

title: Google Slides thumbnail pane missing
steps: Check whether you are presenting or editing.
Return to editing mode and look along the left edge for the slide pane.
If the pane is collapsed, use its normal expand control if available.
why: The slide pane helps navigate and reorder slides.

title: Google Slides speaker notes
steps: Open your slide in editing view.
Look for the notes pane below the slide and expand it if needed.
Enter your own speaking reminders there.
why: Speaker notes are separate from projected slide content.

title: Google Slides skip a slide
steps: Check the thumbnail for a skipped-slide indicator.
Use its context menu to inspect Skip slide if available.
Unskip only if the slide should appear in the assignment.
why: A skipped slide remains in the file but is omitted from presentation playback.

title: Google Slides text box is cut off
steps: Select the text box border.
Resize the box or adjust font size according to directions.
Check the slide in presentation view to make sure text fits.
why: Text boxes may extend outside a slide or clip content.

title: Google Slides move a text box
steps: Click the border of the text box rather than inside the words.
Drag it to the intended location.
Release and check that nearby objects are not covered.
why: Selecting a box border moves the object instead of editing the text.

title: Google Slides text appears behind a picture
steps: Select the picture or text box.
Use Arrange > Order to bring the intended object forward or send the blocking object backward.
Check the text is readable.
why: Object stacking controls what appears in front.

title: Google Slides insert an image
steps: Open the slide and choose Insert > Image.
Select an approved source such as Upload from computer or Drive.
Choose the intended file and position it on the slide.
why: Inserting a file places a copy as an object on the slide.

title: Google Slides image looks stretched
steps: Select the image and inspect its proportions.
Undo the last resize if it caused the problem.
Resize using a corner handle and compare it with your original.
why: Changing only width or height can distort a picture.

title: Google Slides mask an image into a shape
steps: Select the inserted image.
Use the arrow beside Crop if available and choose a mask shape.
Adjust the visible crop and confirm.
why: A mask changes the visible outline of an image without requiring a new file.

title: Google Slides rotate an object
steps: Select the object.
Use its rotation handle or Arrange > Rotate.
Adjust it to the intended angle and check the slide edges.
why: Rotation changes object orientation rather than slide orientation.

title: Google Slides insert a shape
steps: Choose Insert > Shape or the toolbar Shape control.
Select the required shape and drag on the slide.
Use fill and border controls to format it.
why: Shapes are editable objects, not imported images.

title: Google Slides shape fill color
steps: Select the shape itself.
Open Fill color in the toolbar.
Choose a suitable color or transparent fill according to the design.
why: Fill controls the interior of a shape.

title: Google Slides shape border color
steps: Select the shape.
Choose Border color, weight or dash style from the toolbar if shown.
Check contrast with the fill and background.
why: A border is separate from the shape's fill.

title: Google Slides insert a line or arrow
steps: Use Insert > Line or its toolbar menu.
Select a line or arrow and drag between the intended points.
Use line formatting controls to make it readable.
why: Lines connect or emphasize information without being text boxes.

title: Google Slides align several objects
steps: Hold Shift while selecting the objects you want aligned.
Open Arrange > Align and select the alignment needed.
Check that all objects remain on the slide.
why: Aligning uses a consistent edge or center rather than eyeballing positions.

title: Google Slides space objects evenly
steps: Select three or more intended objects.
Use Arrange > Distribute horizontally or vertically if available.
Check spacing and undo if the result is not what you wanted.
why: Distribution spaces selected objects evenly.

title: Google Slides group objects together
steps: Select two or more objects using Shift-click.
Choose Arrange > Group if available.
Move the group and inspect its components.
why: Grouping lets related objects move as a unit.

title: Google Slides cannot edit a grouped object
steps: Select the group and inspect Arrange > Ungroup.
Ungroup only your own editable objects if needed.
Edit the component and regroup when appropriate.
why: An object inside a group may be harder to select independently.

title: Google Slides copy an object to another slide
aliases: slides copy picture to another slide
steps: Select the object border and press Ctrl + C.
Select the destination slide thumbnail and press Ctrl + V.
Check placement and avoid copying unwanted objects.
why: Copying an object does not duplicate the entire slide.

title: Google Slides insert a table
steps: Choose Insert > Table and select rows and columns.
Resize the table to fit the slide.
Enter your own information and check readability in slideshow mode.
why: Tables on slides need enough space for projected text.

title: Google Slides link text or object
steps: Select your own text or object.
Use Insert > Link or Ctrl + K and choose an approved URL or slide destination.
Check the link before presenting.
why: Links can point outside the presentation or to another slide.

title: Google Slides add a transition
steps: Select the slide and find Transition in the toolbar or Slide menu.
Choose the assigned effect and preview it.
Use effects sparingly and follow the teacher's directions.
why: Transitions occur between slides, not on individual objects.

title: Google Slides animate an object
steps: Select the intended object.
Use the Animation option in the Insert or context menu if offered, or the Motion panel.
Choose an approved effect and preview its order.
why: Animations affect individual objects within a slide.

title: Google Slides animation starts too early
steps: Open the Motion or animation panel.
Inspect the object's start condition, such as On click or After previous.
Preview the slide after correcting timing.
why: Timing determines when an object animation plays.

title: Google Slides exit slideshow
steps: Press Esc to leave the presentation.
Return to the editing tab if a new tab opened.
Do not close the entire browser if other work remains open.
why: Presentation mode hides editing controls.

title: Google Slides presentation starts on wrong slide
steps: Select the first slide thumbnail before starting if you want the beginning.
Use the Slideshow button or its available start option.
Check the projected first slide.
why: Some presentation controls start from the currently selected slide.

title: Google Slides video will not play
steps: Check that the teacher-approved video is accessible with your school account.
Try its normal playback control in an appropriate view.
Report blocked or unavailable content; do not change site restrictions.
why: Playback may depend on network access and video permissions.

title: Google Slides audio unavailable
steps: Check your device volume and the slide's approved audio object.
Verify the associated audio file is accessible to your account.
Ask your teacher if playback is blocked or the file is missing.
why: Embedded audio may depend on a separate Drive file.

title: Google Slides download one slide as PNG
steps: Select the specific slide thumbnail.
Use File > Download and choose PNG image if available.
Open the saved image and verify it is the intended slide.
why: Image export generally applies to the current slide.

title: Google Slides download as PDF
steps: Open your own presentation.
Choose File > Download > PDF Document if offered.
Preview the PDF and make sure the required slides appear in order.
why: A PDF does not preserve interactive slide animations.

title: Google Slides download PowerPoint copy
steps: Use File > Download > Microsoft PowerPoint if the assignment requests it.
Keep the original in Drive.
If your teacher provides an approved viewer, check whether the exported layouts remain intact.
why: Conversion can change fonts or effects on some slides.

title: Google Slides image blurry when presented
steps: Inspect the image at actual presentation size.
Check whether the source image was already small or compressed.
Replace it with an approved higher-resolution source if the assignment permits.
why: Stretching a small image cannot create missing detail.

title: Google Slides printing too many pages
steps: Use File > Print settings and preview if available.
Check the handout layout and page count required by your teacher.
Cancel unless printing is authorized.
why: A handout layout can place several slides on one page.

title: Google Sheets select one cell
steps: Click the intended cell and look for its highlighted border.
Check the column letter and row number.
Type only your own required data or use the formula bar to edit.
why: A cell is one intersection of a column and row.

title: Google Sheets select a range
steps: Click and drag across the intended rectangular range.
Check the highlighted start and end cells.
Apply formatting only after confirming all selected cells.
why: A range contains multiple cells, such as A1:A5.

title: Google Sheets edit a cell without replacing it
steps: Double-click your own cell or select it and click the formula bar.
Place the cursor at the part you intend to change.
Press Enter when finished and check the value.
why: Typing immediately into a selected cell may replace its contents.

title: Google Sheets insert a row
steps: Select the row number near the intended location.
Use the context menu to insert a row above or below.
Check any associated formulas and headings.
why: Inserting rows shifts existing cells rather than overwriting them.

title: Google Sheets insert a column
steps: Select the column letter near the desired location.
Use the context menu to insert a column left or right.
Check that related data remains aligned.
why: A column groups data vertically.

title: Google Sheets column too narrow
steps: Move the pointer to the boundary between column letters.
Drag it to change width or double-click the boundary to fit contents if appropriate.
Check the header and neighboring data.
why: Changing column width affects every cell in that column.

title: Google Sheets change row height
steps: Find the boundary between the relevant row numbers.
Drag the boundary to increase or decrease height.
Check that wrapped text remains visible.
why: Row height determines the vertical space for a row.

title: Google Sheets wrap long text
steps: Select the intended cells.
Use Format > Wrapping > Wrap or the toolbar wrapping control.
Check whether the rows expanded enough to show all text.
why: Wrapping displays long content on multiple lines inside a cell.

title: Google Sheets align text inside cells
steps: Select the cells that need formatting.
Use the horizontal or vertical alignment toolbar control.
Choose the teacher-requested alignment.
why: Cell formatting changes appearance without changing values.

title: Google Sheets apply cell fill color
steps: Select the cells to highlight.
Use the Fill color control to choose a suitable color.
Check that the text remains readable.
why: Fill changes the cell background, not the actual value.

title: Google Sheets add borders to cells
steps: Select the intended range.
Open the Borders toolbar control and choose the required edges.
Preview the grid and check readability.
why: Cell borders differ from default gridlines.

title: Google Sheets numbers display as dates
steps: Check the cell contents in the formula bar.
If the entry should be a number or text, undo the unwanted conversion if possible.
Use the teacher-required format and re-enter your own value if needed.
why: Automatic formatting may interpret some input as a date.

title: Google Sheets leading zero disappears
steps: Select the cell or column before entering the value.
If it is an identifier rather than a number, use Format > Number > Plain text if appropriate.
Re-enter your own value and check it displays correctly.
why: Numeric formatting can omit zeros at the beginning of identifiers.

title: Google Sheets percentage formatting
steps: Check the actual cell value in the formula bar.
Choose Format > Number > Percent only if the data represents a proportion.
Check the result against your own intended value.
why: Percent formatting displays 0.25 as 25%; it does not independently calculate a ratio.

title: Google Sheets decimal places
steps: Select the numeric cells.
Use the increase or decrease decimal places controls.
Check that the displayed precision meets the assignment.
why: Display rounding does not normally change the underlying value.

title: Google Sheets currency formatting
steps: Select the numeric cells.
Use the currency format control or Format > Number.
Check that the symbols and decimal places match the assigned data.
why: Currency format changes presentation rather than the amount.

title: Google Sheets freeze header row
steps: Open View > Freeze.
Choose the required number of header rows for your own sheet.
Scroll down and check that the headings stay visible.
why: Frozen rows stay on-screen while scrolling.

title: Google Sheets find a sheet tab
steps: Look at the sheet tabs along the bottom of the file.
Scroll the tab strip or use the available sheet list control.
Open the assigned tab; ask before accessing restricted sheets.
why: One spreadsheet file can contain multiple worksheets.

title: Google Sheets rename a sheet tab
steps: Double-click your own worksheet tab or use its menu.
Enter the name required for the assignment.
Check other tabs are unchanged.
why: A sheet tab name is separate from the spreadsheet filename.

title: Google Sheets add another sheet
steps: Click the plus button near the sheet tabs.
Name the new sheet according to directions.
Enter your own approved data there.
why: A new sheet adds another grid to the same file.

title: Google Sheets formula starts with equals
steps: Select the result cell in your own sheet.
Start a formula with an equals sign and enter the operation required by the lesson.
Press Enter and examine the result; ask your teacher about the actual math.
why: The equals sign tells Sheets to interpret an expression as a formula.

title: Google Sheets formula is showing as text
steps: Check whether the cell has Plain text formatting or begins with an apostrophe.
If appropriate, choose the required number format and re-enter your own formula.
Ask your teacher if the formula still does not evaluate.
why: A text-formatted cell may treat a formula as literal text.

title: Google Sheets formula parse error
steps: Select the error cell and read its error message.
Review matching parentheses, cell references and the required separators in your own formula.
Correct only the syntax you understand or ask the teacher.
why: A parse error indicates that the expression cannot be interpreted.

title: Google Sheets REF error
steps: Select the cell with the reference error.
Inspect the formula bar for a deleted or invalid cell reference.
Use Undo if you just removed needed data, or ask your teacher how to repair the reference.
why: A formula may refer to cells that no longer exist.

title: Google Sheets DIV zero error
steps: Select the error cell and inspect the referenced divisor.
Check whether that cell is blank or contains zero.
Ask your teacher how the assignment handles missing or zero values.
why: Division by zero is undefined; do not change real data just to hide an error.

title: Google Sheets VALUE error
steps: Read the cell's displayed error details.
Check whether a numeric formula refers to text or an unexpected value.
Correct only a genuine input mistake in your own data.
why: Some formulas require particular kinds of data.

title: Google Sheets NAME error
steps: Select the formula cell and inspect the function name.
Compare its spelling with the teacher-provided example or built-in function hint.
Ask about any unfamiliar name.
why: An unrecognized name may indicate a misspelled function or reference.

title: Google Sheets circular dependency warning
steps: Read the warning and inspect the formula's referenced cells.
Check whether the result cell is also part of its own formula range.
Ask the teacher how to correct the reference; do not change calculation settings.
why: A circular dependency can make a result depend on itself.

title: Google Sheets copy a formula down
steps: Select the cell containing your own working formula.
Drag its small fill handle down the intended range.
Check a copied formula to see whether cell references changed as intended.
why: Relative references usually shift when a formula is filled.

title: Google Sheets absolute cell reference
steps: Look at the teacher's example of relative and absolute references.
In a practice formula, note that a dollar sign before a row or column keeps that part fixed when copied.
Compare your copied references with the expected pattern.
why: Fixed references help preserve a constant cell location during copying.

title: Google Sheets formula range includes wrong cells
steps: Select the result cell and inspect the formula bar or colored reference outlines.
Compare the selected range with the data required in the lesson.
Correct the reference yourself with guidance from your teacher.
why: A formula can be valid but refer to the wrong cells.

title: Google Sheets sort a table without mixing rows
steps: Use only your own authorized table; select the complete data range including related columns.
Open Data > Sort range and identify whether the range contains a header if offered.
Choose the required sort column and verify each record stayed together.
why: Sorting just one column can separate related information.

title: Google Sheets filter hides rows
steps: Look for filter icons in the header and missing row numbers.
Check the active filter criteria without altering shared data.
Ask your teacher before changing a shared filter; adjust only your own authorized filter.
why: Filtered rows are hidden from the view, not necessarily deleted.

title: Google Sheets create a chart
steps: Select your own prepared data range including appropriate labels.
Choose Insert > Chart.
Use the chart editor to select the chart type required by the assignment and review the result.
why: Charts visualize selected data; a wrong range can produce misleading results.

title: Google Sheets chart has wrong labels
steps: Select your chart and open its chart editor.
Check the selected data range and header or label options.
Compare the labels with your original data.
why: Chart labels depend on the range and setup choices.

title: Google Sheets change chart title
steps: Select your own chart and open the chart editor.
Find chart and axis title controls under Customize if available.
Enter your own descriptive title required by the lesson.
why: A clear chart title identifies what the data represents.

title: Google Sheets print one selected range
steps: Select the cells needed for the assignment.
Open File > Print and choose Selected cells if available.
Check the preview and cancel unless printing is approved.
why: Printing only the chosen range avoids unnecessary pages.

title: Google Sheets download CSV
steps: Select the worksheet you need.
Use File > Download > Comma-separated values if required.
Keep the editable spreadsheet and verify the exported file name.
why: CSV stores plain table data from a sheet, not its charts or formatting.

title: Google Sheets download Excel copy
steps: Use File > Download > Microsoft Excel if the teacher requires it.
Keep your original Google spreadsheet.
Open the copy in an approved application if available to check compatibility.
why: Export conversion may affect certain formulas or formatting.

title: Google Forms required question missing
steps: Scroll through the form and look for an unanswered required field.
Read the question and enter your own response.
Try submitting again only after all required items are complete.
why: A required question must have a valid response before submission.

title: Google Forms answer has invalid format
steps: Read the validation message beneath the field.
Check the requested format, such as a number or school-approved address.
Correct your own entry without inventing information.
why: Forms can enforce response formatting rules.

title: Google Forms cannot go to next section
steps: Check the current section for required questions or invalid response warnings.
Complete the required fields with your own answers.
Use Next again; tell the teacher if it remains stuck.
why: Multi-section forms may require valid answers before advancing.

title: Google Forms checkbox versus radio button
steps: Read the question directions.
Round option controls usually allow one selection; square checkboxes may allow multiple selections.
Choose your own answer according to the question.
why: Different question controls have different selection behavior.

title: Google Forms file upload question
steps: Check the requested file type and size.
Use the normal Add file control and select your own approved file.
Wait for it to finish, then complete the form yourself.
why: File upload availability depends on form and school account permissions.

title: Google Forms says school account required
steps: Check the account shown on the form.
Use the teacher-assigned school account through approved sign-in steps.
If it is still inaccessible, ask the form owner.
why: School forms may restrict access to an organization.

title: Google Forms not accepting responses
steps: Read the message at the top of the form.
Confirm the link is the teacher's current assignment.
Ask the teacher whether the form should be reopened.
why: Only the form owner decides whether responses are accepted.

title: Google Forms already responded
steps: Read the confirmation or restriction notice.
If an approved Edit response link is available, follow the teacher's directions.
Otherwise ask your teacher rather than using another account.
why: Some forms accept only one response per person.

title: Google Forms unsure whether submission worked
steps: Look for the form's submission confirmation screen.
If it is not visible, check whether an error message appeared.
Ask your teacher to verify before sending duplicate responses.
why: A confirmation usually indicates a response was received.

title: Google Forms edit submitted response
steps: Use an Edit response link only if it was provided and your teacher permits changes.
Correct your own response and submit again as directed.
If the link is not offered, ask the teacher.
why: Response editing depends on the form owner's settings.

title: Google Forms quiz score not shown
steps: Check the confirmation page for an approved score-viewing option.
If no score is available, wait for the teacher's feedback.
Do not attempt to inspect hidden answers or bypass quiz settings.
why: Quiz results may be released later by the teacher.

title: Google Forms form resets after closing
steps: Reopen the assigned form with the correct school account.
Check whether any draft is still available.
If not, tell your teacher and re-enter your own answers only as directed.
why: Draft saving may depend on form settings and account access.

title: Google Meet microphone muted
steps: Check the microphone icon in the meeting controls.
Unmute only when permitted and when it is your turn.
If it remains unavailable, tell the teacher using an approved communication method.
why: A muted microphone does not send your audio.

title: Google Meet camera covered
steps: Check whether your device has a camera privacy cover and whether the teacher expects video.
Open the cover only if authorized and check the meeting camera icon.
Ask for help if video is still unavailable.
why: A camera cover physically blocks the image.

title: Google Meet captions
steps: Look for the captions button in the meeting toolbar.
Turn captions on if available to help you follow the meeting.
Keep any required accessibility features in place.
why: Live captions may contain errors and are not a perfect transcript.

title: Google Meet cannot join meeting
steps: Open the teacher-provided meeting link with your school account.
Check the displayed waiting or access message.
Ask your teacher if admission is needed or the link is outdated.
why: Meeting access is controlled by the host and school policy.

title: Google Meet echo
steps: Mute your microphone when not speaking.
If permitted, use the classroom-approved headphones.
Tell the teacher if the echo continues; do not change another person's equipment.
why: Microphones can pick up sound from nearby speakers.

title: Google Meet share a school assignment
steps: Share only if the teacher asks you to present.
Use the normal presentation control and choose only the specific approved tab or window if available.
Stop sharing when done and avoid showing private information.
why: Sharing a whole screen can expose unrelated tabs or notices.

title: Google Drawings add a shape
steps: Open your own drawing and choose the Shape toolbar control.
Select the desired shape and drag on the canvas.
