Use its handles and fill controls to make your own design.
why: Drawing shapes remain editable objects.

title: Google Drawings object hidden behind another
steps: Select the relevant object.
Use Arrange > Order to reposition it in the stack.
Check the visible result.
why: Objects can overlap in front-to-back order.

title: Google Drawings export image
steps: Use File > Download and select the required format, such as PNG if offered.
Find the downloaded file and preview it.
Keep your editable drawing in Drive.
why: Downloading creates a separate copy in the chosen format.

title: Google Drawings insert a text box
steps: Choose the Text box toolbar control and drag on the canvas.
Type your own text and apply required formatting.
Resize the box to keep text readable.
why: A text box can be positioned independently of shapes.

title: Options bar missing
steps: Open Window > Options.
Select the tool you are using and look along the top of the document area.
If the bar is still absent, ask your teacher before changing the workspace.
why: The Options bar shows controls for the active tool.

title: Toolbar missing
steps: Choose Window > Tools.
Look for the toolbar along the left side.
If only one tool is missing, look under a related tool by holding its icon.
why: Tools can be hidden without being removed from Photoshop.

title: All panels disappeared
steps: Press Tab once while not typing in a text box.
Check whether the toolbar and panels return.
If not, open the specific panel from Window.
why: Tab toggles panel visibility.

title: Find a hidden tool
steps: Look for a related tool icon in the toolbar.
Click and hold that icon to reveal the tool group.
Select the tool by name.
why: Several tools share the same toolbar slot.

title: Switch between open images
steps: Find the document tabs above the canvas.
Click the tab showing your project filename.
Check the filename before continuing edits.
why: Each open document has its own layers and history.

title: Return to normal screen mode
steps: Finish any active text editing first.
Press F until the normal menu and document tabs return.
If a tool dialog is open, cancel it safely instead of repeatedly pressing keys.
why: Photoshop cycles through screen modes.

title: Zoom to fit entire image
steps: Choose View > Fit on Screen or press Ctrl+0 on Windows.
Check the entire canvas.
Use the Zoom tool to inspect details afterward.
why: Fitting the view changes magnification, not image size.

title: View actual pixels
steps: Choose View > 100% or press Ctrl+1 on Windows.
Inspect an edge or detail.
Return to Fit on Screen when finished.
why: At 100%, zoom is useful for checking image quality.

title: Move around zoomed canvas
steps: Hold Space while dragging on the canvas, outside text editing.
Release Space to return to your previous tool.
Fit the image on screen if you become lost.
why: Panning moves the view, not your artwork.

title: Navigator panel
steps: Choose Window > Navigator.
Drag the preview frame to inspect a different part of the image.
Adjust the zoom with its slider as needed.
why: The Navigator shows the location of your current view.

title: History panel
steps: Choose Window > History.
Locate the recent actions in the list.
If you need to undo, review the previous state and avoid clearing history.
why: History tracks recent changes in this open document.

title: Undo recent edit
steps: Press Ctrl+Z on Windows once.
Check whether the unwanted change was reversed.
Repeat only as needed; stop if earlier correct work begins disappearing.
why: Undo reverses recent editing actions.

title: Redo an undone edit
steps: Choose Edit > Redo or press Ctrl+Shift+Z on Windows.
Inspect the result before repeating.
Save your project once the correct edit is restored.
why: Redo restores an action you just undid when available.

title: Rulers not visible
steps: Choose View > Rulers or press Ctrl+R on Windows.
Look at the top and left of the canvas.
Use the ruler as a placement reference.
why: Rulers display document measurements.

title: Show or hide guides
steps: Choose View > Show > Guides.
Inspect whether the lines are visible.
Do not delete guides required by your teacher.
why: Guides are alignment references, not printed artwork.

title: Show grid in Photoshop
steps: Choose View > Show > Grid.
Check the grid across the canvas.
Toggle it off with the same menu only if your teacher does not require it.
why: The grid assists precise placement without becoming artwork.

title: Photoshop canvas rotated
steps: Select the Rotate View tool, usually grouped with the Hand tool.
Choose Reset View in the Options bar.
Check the image orientation before making any actual rotation.
why: Rotate View changes the viewing angle rather than the image pixels.

title: Photoshop cursor is a crosshair
steps: Press Caps Lock once when not typing text.
Move the brush over the canvas and inspect its cursor.
If the problem persists, ask your teacher instead of changing preferences.
why: Caps Lock can toggle precise cursors.

title: Photoshop frozen
steps: Stop clicking and give the program time to finish its current operation.
If it responds, save your editable file.
If it remains frozen, tell your teacher before closing it.
why: Repeated input can queue more work and unsaved edits may be lost.

title: Photoshop scratch disk full
steps: Stop the operation and note the exact message.
Save your work if Photoshop still allows it.
Ask your teacher or IT staff; do not delete files or change storage preferences.
why: Scratch disk problems need authorized storage support.

title: Create a new blank layer
steps: Open Window > Layers if needed.
Click the plus icon at the bottom of the Layers panel.
Name the layer and confirm it is selected before editing.
why: Separate layers keep edits independent.

title: Name a layer
steps: Double-click the layer name in the Layers panel.
Type a short descriptive name.
Press Enter to confirm.
why: Clear names help you locate artwork later.

title: Duplicate a layer
steps: Select the layer in the Layers panel.
Press Ctrl+J on Windows.
Rename the copy and check that the original remains underneath.
why: A copy lets you experiment without changing the original.

title: Move layer above another
steps: Find both layers in the Layers panel.
Drag the desired layer above the other one.
Observe the canvas to check whether it now appears in front.
why: Layer stacking controls which pixels cover others.

title: Hide a layer temporarily
steps: Locate the layer in the Layers panel.
Click its eye icon to hide it.
Click the same space to reveal it again.
why: Visibility changes do not erase layer contents.

title: Layer is locked
steps: Select the intended layer and inspect the lock symbol.
If it is your editable layer, check which lock is enabled and unlock it if allowed.
For an original background, duplicate it instead and work on the copy.
why: Locks protect layer content or position.

title: Layer opacity too low
steps: Select the layer in the Layers panel.
Check its Opacity value near the top.
Raise it to the intended level and inspect the image.
why: Layer opacity controls the visibility of the whole layer.

title: Layer fill versus opacity
steps: Select a layer with a visible layer style.
Compare the Fill and Opacity controls in the Layers panel.
Undo any test changes after observing the difference.
why: Fill can reduce layer pixels while leaving many styles visible; Opacity affects the whole layer.

title: Group several layers
steps: Select the related layers using Shift or Ctrl clicks.
Press Ctrl+G on Windows.
Name the group and expand it to confirm the contents.
why: Groups organize related objects without merging them.

title: Find layers inside a group
steps: Locate the folder icon in the Layers panel.
Click the small arrow beside it.
Select the needed layer inside the expanded group.
why: Collapsed groups hide rows, not the artwork itself.

title: Select multiple layers
steps: Click the first layer in the Layers panel.
Hold Ctrl while clicking nonadjacent layers, or Shift for a range.
Confirm only the intended rows are highlighted before editing.
why: Multiple selected layers may move together.

title: Align several layers
steps: Select the layers to align.
Select the Move tool and find the alignment controls in its Options bar.
Choose the appropriate edge or center and inspect the arrangement.
why: Alignment uses the selected layers as references.

title: Auto-select moves wrong layer
steps: Select the intended layer directly in the Layers panel.
Choose the Move tool and inspect Auto-Select in its Options bar.
Turn Auto-Select off if it is selecting unwanted layers, then test a small move.
why: Auto-Select can choose the top object under your pointer.

title: Delete an unwanted layer safely
steps: Identify the correct layer by toggling its visibility first.
If unsure, leave it hidden instead of deleting.
If it is definitely unnecessary, select it and use the Layers panel trash icon; undo if needed.
why: Confirming visibility helps avoid deleting the wrong work.

title: Layer thumbnail versus mask thumbnail
steps: Look for the small border around the active thumbnail in the Layers panel.
Click the image thumbnail to edit image pixels or the mask thumbnail to edit visibility.
Check the active thumbnail again before painting.
why: The image and mask are separate editable targets.

title: Convert a layer to Smart Object
steps: Select the layer you want to preserve.
Right-click it and choose Convert to Smart Object.
Keep your editable original and inspect the new Smart Object badge.
why: Smart Objects can preserve source data during many transformations.

title: Smart Object cannot be directly edited
steps: Check for the Smart Object badge on the layer thumbnail.
For painting, add a blank layer above it; for a mask, select the mask itself.
Ask your teacher before rasterizing or editing the source document.
why: A Smart Object protects its source pixels from direct edits.

title: Edit embedded Smart Object contents
steps: Double-click the Smart Object image thumbnail.
When the source document opens, make your approved edit there.
Save that source document and return to the main file.
why: Saving embedded source changes updates the parent composition.

title: Clipping mask not working
steps: Put the layer to be clipped directly above the base layer.
Right-click the upper layer and choose Create Clipping Mask.
Check that the base layer has visible opaque pixels.
why: The upper layer is limited to the visible shape of the base layer.

title: Release a clipping mask
steps: Select the clipped layer in the Layers panel.
Right-click and choose Release Clipping Mask.
Inspect the full layer and undo if it was intended to stay clipped.
why: Releasing a clipping mask reveals previously clipped pixels.

title: Merge layers versus keep editable
steps: Save the layered PSD first.
If you need a flattened deliverable, export a PNG or JPG instead of flattening the original.
Only merge layers when your teacher specifically requests it.
why: Merging reduces separate editing options.

title: Select Subject
steps: Select the image layer containing your subject.
Choose Select > Subject, if available.
Inspect the selected outline before using a mask.
why: Automatic selection can miss fine details and needs review.

title: Object Selection tool
steps: Choose the Object Selection tool from the toolbar group.
Use its rectangle or lasso mode to mark the target, or select a detected object if shown.
Check the resulting outline and refine as needed.
why: Object Selection targets an individual object within an image.

title: Quick Selection tool
steps: Choose Quick Selection in the toolbar.
Drag inside the object you want selected.
Use its subtract option to remove unwanted areas.
why: Quick Selection expands using nearby color and edge information.

title: Magic Wand tool
steps: Find the Magic Wand under its selection tool group.
Click the desired color region on the correct image layer.
Check the outline; adjust Tolerance in the Options bar if needed.
why: The Magic Wand selects pixels with related colors.

title: Magic Wand selects too much
steps: Choose Select > Deselect.
Lower Tolerance in the Magic Wand Options bar.
Click the intended area again and inspect the selection.
why: Lower tolerance limits the range of similar colors.

title: Magic Wand selects disconnected areas
steps: Select the Magic Wand.
Check Contiguous in its Options bar.
Enable it if you want only neighboring similar pixels, then select again.
why: Contiguous limits selection to connected regions.

title: Rectangular Marquee
steps: Choose Rectangular Marquee.
Drag from one corner of the area to the opposite corner.
Inspect the outline before editing.
why: Marquee tools create geometric selections.

title: Elliptical Marquee
steps: Hold the Marquee icon and choose Elliptical Marquee.
Drag around the intended oval area.
Hold Shift during a new drag if a circle is needed.
why: The Elliptical Marquee selects rounded areas.

title: Lasso tool
steps: Choose Lasso from the toolbar.
Drag around the desired area and close the loop.
Check the outline before applying an edit.
why: The Lasso lets you define an irregular selection by hand.

title: Polygonal Lasso
steps: Choose Polygonal Lasso in the Lasso group.
Click along the straight edges of your subject.
Click the starting point to close the selection.
why: Straight segments are useful for angular subjects.

title: Magnetic Lasso
steps: Choose Magnetic Lasso.
Trace slowly near a clear object boundary.
Click to place extra points where needed and close the selection.
why: Magnetic Lasso follows strong edges but may miss weak contrast.

title: Add to a selection
steps: Choose a selection tool while your selection is active.
Choose Add to Selection in the Options bar, or hold Shift as appropriate.
Select the missing region and check the combined outline.
why: Adding preserves the original area while including more pixels.

title: Subtract from a selection
steps: Choose a selection tool.
Choose Subtract from Selection in the Options bar, or use Alt as appropriate.
Mark the extra region and check the remaining outline.
why: Subtracting excludes pixels without starting over.

title: Invert a selection
steps: Start with an active selection.
Choose Select > Inverse or press Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows.
Check that the opposite area is outlined before editing.
why: Inverse selects everything that was outside the original selection.

title: Feather a selection
steps: Make a selection first.
Choose Select > Modify > Feather and enter a small amount suitable for your image size.
Preview the resulting edge with a mask on a copy.
why: Feathering softens the transition at a selection boundary.

title: Expand a selection
steps: Make the intended selection.
Choose Select > Modify > Expand.
Use a small pixel value and inspect the new boundary.
why: Expanding grows the selection outward.

title: Contract a selection
steps: Make or refine your selection.
Choose Select > Modify > Contract.
Use a small pixel value and check that needed details remain.
why: Contracting moves the selection boundary inward.

title: Save a selection for later
steps: Make the selection you want to reuse.
Choose Select > Save Selection and give it a descriptive name.
Save your PSD and use Select > Load Selection when needed.
why: Stored selections can be reused in the same document.

title: Select and Mask workspace
steps: Make an initial subject selection.
Choose Select > Select and Mask, if available.
Inspect the preview before changing edge controls.
why: This workspace refines the edges of a selection or mask.

title: Select and Mask preview background
steps: Open Select and Mask.
Choose a View mode that contrasts with the subject, such as On Black or On White.
Switch views to look for missed areas.
why: Different preview backgrounds reveal different edge problems.

title: Refine hair or fur edges
aliases: hair looks bad after cutting out
steps: Open Select and Mask with the subject selected.
Use the Refine Edge Brush lightly over hair or fur boundaries.
Inspect the preview; avoid brushing across large solid interior areas.
why: Fine edge detail often needs separate refinement.

title: Smooth jagged selection
steps: Open Select and Mask.
Increase Smooth gradually while previewing the edge.
Keep the adjustment small enough to preserve important details.
why: Smoothing reduces irregular bumps in a selection boundary.

title: Shift Edge to reduce fringe
steps: Open Select and Mask and choose a contrasting preview.
Try a small negative Shift Edge value.
Inspect hair and fine details before confirming.
why: Moving the edge inward can reduce unwanted background fringe.

title: Output Select and Mask to a layer mask
steps: Open Select and Mask and finish your edge check.
In Output Settings choose Layer Mask or New Layer with Layer Mask as appropriate.
Confirm and inspect the Layers panel.
why: A mask preserves hidden source pixels for later correction.

title: Quick Mask red overlay
steps: Check whether Quick Mask mode is active.
Press Q when not typing text to return to standard selection mode.
Inspect the selection outline before editing.
why: Quick Mask often displays selected or masked areas as an overlay.

title: Selection outline hidden
steps: Check Select menu whether Deselect is available.
Choose View > Extras if selection edges were hidden.
Deselect only if you no longer need the selection.
why: A hidden outline does not necessarily mean the selection is gone.

title: Black white gray mask meanings
steps: Select the layer mask thumbnail.
Use black to hide, white to reveal, and gray for partial visibility.
Test a small stroke and undo if the result is unexpected.
why: A grayscale mask controls visibility without changing source pixels.

title: Restore a masked-out area
steps: Select the mask thumbnail of the correct layer.
Choose a white Brush and paint over the missing region.
Use a smaller brush around detail and inspect the result.
why: White on a layer mask reveals underlying layer content.

title: Hide extra background with a mask
steps: Select the layer mask thumbnail.
Choose a black Brush and paint only over unwanted background areas.
Zoom in to refine the boundary.
why: Black on the mask hides extra pixels without deleting them.

title: Invert a layer mask
steps: Select the actual mask thumbnail, not the image thumbnail.
Press Ctrl+I on Windows.
Inspect whether the intended content is now visible.
why: Inverting a mask swaps its black and white values.

title: Temporarily disable a layer mask
steps: Shift-click the layer mask thumbnail to temporarily disable it.
Inspect the original layer content.
Shift-click again to restore the mask.
why: Disabling the mask is a reversible comparison.

title: View only the layer mask
steps: Alt-click the layer mask thumbnail on Windows.
Inspect the grayscale mask for holes or unwanted patches.
Alt-click again to return to the normal canvas.
why: The mask-only view makes visibility mistakes easier to find.

title: Mask edge too sharp
steps: Select the mask thumbnail.
Open Window > Properties and inspect Feather if available.
Use a small amount and check edges at normal zoom.
why: Mask feathering softens the transition without erasing pixels.

title: Mask too transparent
steps: Select the mask thumbnail and open Properties.
Check the Density slider.
Return it toward 100% if hidden areas are showing through unintentionally.
why: Density controls the strength of a mask.

title: Move image without moving mask
steps: Locate the link icon between the image and mask thumbnails.
Click it to unlink, select the image thumbnail, and move the image carefully.
Re-link when the placement is correct.
why: Unlinking allows independent movement of the image and its mask.

title: Remove mask without deleting pixels
steps: Save your PSD first.
Right-click the mask thumbnail and choose Delete Layer Mask only if you intend to remove it.
If asked, do not choose Apply when you want to retain hidden source pixels.
why: Deleting a mask can restore hidden content; applying it removes masked pixels.

title: Place a photo into a project
steps: Choose File > Place Embedded and select your approved image.
Position and size it using the transform handles.
Confirm the placement and check the new layer.
why: Placed images commonly remain editable Smart Objects.

title: Combine photos into one composition
steps: Open your editable base image.
Place each approved photo on its own layer.
Name the layers and use masks for unwanted backgrounds.
why: Separate layers make compositing revisions easier.

title: Resize a placed object proportionally
steps: Select the object layer and press Ctrl+T on Windows.
Check the proportion-link control in the Options bar; use corner handles with proportions linked.
Press Enter when satisfied, or Esc to cancel.
why: Maintaining proportions prevents unintended stretching.

title: Rotate a single object
steps: Select the intended layer and press Ctrl+T.
Drag outside a corner handle to rotate, or enter an angle if shown.
Confirm when the angle is correct.
why: Free Transform applies to selected layers, not the whole image.

title: Flip one layer horizontally
steps: Select only the intended layer.
Choose Edit > Transform > Flip Horizontal.
Inspect any text and directional lighting before keeping the edit.
why: This mirrors the selected layer rather than the entire canvas.

title: Flip one layer vertically
steps: Select the layer to flip.
Choose Edit > Transform > Flip Vertical.
Inspect the result and undo if it is unintended.
why: Vertical flipping reverses the layer top to bottom.

title: Distort a layer for perspective
steps: Select the layer and choose Edit > Transform > Distort.
Move individual corner handles to align with the target plane.
Confirm only after inspecting the result.
why: Distort adjusts corners independently for perspective matching.

title: Warp a placed object
steps: Select the layer, preferably preserving it as a Smart Object.
Choose Edit > Transform > Warp and adjust the grid gently.
Confirm or cancel after checking the object's shape.
why: Warp bends a layer without moving every point equally.

title: Object partly outside canvas
steps: Select its layer and use Ctrl+T to locate the full transform bounds.
Reposition or scale it without changing the document dimensions.
Confirm that required parts fit inside the canvas.
why: Pixels beyond the canvas are not visible in the final export.

title: Blend a layer with its background
steps: Select the upper layer.
Open the Blend Mode menu in the Layers panel and preview Normal first.
Try an appropriate blend mode on your own image and undo if unsuitable.
why: Blend modes change how upper and lower colors interact.

title: Add a soft contact shadow
steps: Create a separate blank layer below your subject but above the background.
Paint a small soft dark shadow near the actual contact area.
Reduce opacity and compare with the scene lighting.
why: Contact shadows help show where an object meets a surface.

title: Match direction of light
steps: Look at existing shadows and highlights in the background.
Compare the subject's bright and dark sides before changing it.
Use a masked adjustment layer if needed; avoid flipping text or directional details accidentally.
why: Consistent light direction helps a composite look believable.

title: Match subject brightness to background
steps: Select the subject layer.
Add a Brightness/Contrast adjustment above it and clip it to the subject.
Adjust gradually while comparing with the background.
why: A clipped adjustment changes the subject independently.

title: Match sharpness of subject and background
steps: Inspect both subject and background at 100%.
If appropriate, use a small blur on a Smart Object or copied subject layer.
Compare at normal size before keeping the effect.
why: Matching focus helps elements feel like they belong in the same scene.

title: Add a Hue/Saturation adjustment
steps: Select the layer you want to adjust.
Use Layer > New Adjustment Layer > Hue/Saturation.
Adjust the sliders and inspect the affected area.
why: Adjustment layers remain editable.

title: Hue change affects entire image
steps: Place the Hue/Saturation adjustment above the intended layer.
Use a clipping mask for one layer or a layer mask for a selected region.
Inspect adjacent objects to ensure their colors remain unchanged.
why: Masks and clipping control the area affected by an adjustment.

title: Colorize a selected area
steps: Select only the intended portion of your own image.
Add a Hue/Saturation adjustment and try Colorize if needed.
Refine its mask and preserve natural light and dark details.
why: The selected area becomes the adjustment mask.

title: Brightness and Contrast
steps: Add a Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer.
Move Brightness a little at a time and compare detail in highlights and shadows.
Adjust Contrast cautiously, then toggle visibility to compare.
why: Adjustments can improve visibility without replacing the source pixels.

title: Levels adjustment
steps: Add a Levels adjustment layer.
Inspect the histogram and move the input sliders slightly.
Avoid losing important highlight or shadow detail.
why: Levels adjusts the range and midpoint of image tones.

title: Curves adjustment
steps: Add a Curves adjustment layer.
Make a small adjustment near the middle of the curve.
Toggle visibility to compare and undo if tones become unnatural.
why: Curves provides precise control of brightness across tonal ranges.

title: Photo looks too saturated
steps: Add a Hue/Saturation adjustment layer.
Reduce Saturation gradually.
Compare against the original using the eye icon.
why: Excess saturation can hide natural color differences.

title: Use Vibrance
steps: Add a Vibrance adjustment layer.
Increase or decrease Vibrance gradually.
Check skin tones and other sensitive colors before keeping it.
why: Vibrance generally changes less-saturated colors more strongly.

title: Make a reversible black and white image
steps: Add a Black & White adjustment layer.
Adjust the color sliders to control grayscale tone if needed.
Hide the adjustment to return to the original colors.
why: An adjustment retains the original color data.

title: Unexpected black and white image
steps: Check whether a Black & White or other adjustment layer is visible.
Check whether the active thumbnail is a layer mask.
If Image > Mode shows Grayscale, ask your teacher before converting; converting cannot recover lost colors.
why: Several different conditions can cause a grayscale appearance.

title: Color Balance adjustment
steps: Add a Color Balance adjustment layer.
Make small changes to correct an unwanted color tint.
Compare neutral areas and toggle the adjustment off to check.
why: Color Balance shifts the relationship between color channels.

title: Clip adjustment to one layer
steps: Move the adjustment directly above the layer you want to affect.
Right-click the adjustment and choose Create Clipping Mask.
Check that other layers remain unchanged.
why: A clipped adjustment is restricted to its base layer.

title: Edit existing adjustment later
steps: Select the adjustment icon thumbnail, not its mask.
Open Window > Properties if the controls are not visible.
Change the desired slider while observing the canvas.
why: Adjustment layer settings can be revised after creation.

title: Fill with a solid color layer
steps: Choose Layer > New Fill Layer > Solid Color.
Choose a color and confirm.
Place the fill layer below artwork for a background or use its mask to limit coverage.
why: A fill layer stays editable after the color is chosen.

title: Gradient fill layer
steps: Choose Layer > New Fill Layer > Gradient.
Choose the gradient colors, style and angle.
Adjust the layer order and mask if needed.
why: Gradient fill layers retain editable gradient settings.

title: Brush size too large or small
steps: Choose the Brush tool.
Use the bracket keys [ and ] or the size control in the Options bar.
Test a small stroke on a separate layer.
why: Brush diameter determines the area covered per stroke.

title: Brush edge too hard
steps: Choose the Brush tool and open its brush preset controls.
Lower Hardness for a soft edge or increase it for a crisp edge.
Test on a spare layer.
why: Hardness controls the transition around the brush edge.

title: Brush strokes are faint
steps: Check Brush Opacity and Flow in the Options bar.
Check the target layer's Opacity and whether a mask is selected.
Test the brush on a new blank layer using known colors.
why: Both brush and layer controls affect visible paint strength.

title: Brush paints the wrong color
steps: Check the foreground color swatch.
Click it and choose the intended color.
If editing a mask, select the image thumbnail before using color.
why: Masks accept grayscale rather than ordinary color painting.

title: Swap foreground and background colors
steps: Finish any text editing.
Press X to swap foreground and background swatches.
Check the foreground swatch before painting.
why: Swapping is useful when alternating black and white mask strokes.

title: Reset foreground and background colors
steps: Finish any text editing.
Press D to return to default foreground/background colors.
Inspect the swatches and press X if the opposite color is needed.
why: Default colors are useful for mask editing and basic brush tests.

title: Eyedropper picks color
steps: Choose the Eyedropper tool.
Click an appropriate color in the image.
Look at the foreground swatch before painting.
why: The Eyedropper samples color from the image.

title: Paint only inside selection
steps: Make a selection of the region you want to modify.
Create a separate blank layer and paint within the selected region.
Deselect after you finish and inspect the result.
why: Active selections restrict many painting operations.

title: Paint Bucket fills too much
steps: Undo the unwanted fill.
Check Tolerance and Contiguous in the Paint Bucket Options bar.
Try a smaller tolerance or make a controlled selection first.
why: The Paint Bucket fills related pixels according to its options.

title: Create a rectangle shape
steps: Choose the Rectangle tool.
Choose Shape mode and set Fill and Stroke in the Options bar.
Drag on the canvas and check the new shape layer.
why: Shape layers retain editable vector properties.

title: Shape has no fill
steps: Select the shape layer and its shape tool.
Choose a Fill color in the Options bar or Properties panel.
Check whether Stroke or Fill is set to None.
why: Fill controls the interior; Stroke controls the boundary.

title: Change shape outline
steps: Select the shape layer.
Choose Stroke color and width from shape controls.
Inspect at normal zoom.
why: A shape stroke is independently editable from its fill.

title: Rounded rectangle corners
steps: Select your rectangle shape layer.
Inspect the corner radius controls in Properties.
Adjust the radius and check that the shape still fits your design.
why: Corner settings preserve editable shape geometry.

title: Spot Healing Brush
steps: Create a new blank retouch layer and select Spot Healing Brush.
Enable Sample All Layers if available.
Use small strokes on harmless dust or minor marks and compare with the original.
why: Spot Healing blends a small region with neighboring image detail.

title: Healing Brush with sample
steps: Select Healing Brush and create a separate retouch layer.
Set Sample to Current & Below or All Layers as appropriate.
Alt-click a clean nearby source on Windows, then paint over the small mark.
why: Healing combines sampled texture with surrounding tones.

title: Clone Stamp tool
steps: Create a separate retouch layer and select Clone Stamp.
Set Sample to Current & Below or All Layers as appropriate.
Alt-click a nearby source on Windows and paint a short stroke; resample often.
why: Clone Stamp copies source pixels directly.

title: Clone Stamp does nothing
steps: Check that the target layer is visible and editable.
Check the Sample option and Alt-click a valid source point.
Try a short stroke on a new retouch layer.
why: Cloning needs both a source and an editable destination.

title: Remove small dust spots safely
steps: Create a separate retouch layer.
Use Spot Healing with a brush only slightly larger than each spot.
Toggle the retouch layer off and on to inspect your work.
why: Small localized edits preserve more original texture.

title: Retouch repeats obvious pattern
steps: Inspect the retouched area at 100%.
Undo or mask repeated strokes and choose varied nearby sample points.
Blend using small strokes and compare at normal size.
why: Reusing the same source can create obvious repetitions.

title: Blur a small region
steps: Duplicate the image layer or preserve the original beneath it.
Choose Blur tool and use a low Strength setting.
Brush lightly over the intended region and compare.
why: Selective blurring reduces detail in a localized area.

title: Sharpen a small region
steps: Duplicate the image layer before editing.
Use the Sharpen tool with a low Strength setting.
Apply sparingly and inspect at 100% for halos or noise.
why: Sharpening increases local contrast but cannot restore missing detail.

title: Non-destructive Gaussian Blur
steps: Select a copy or Smart Object layer.
Choose Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur.
Preview a small radius and adjust or cancel.
why: A Smart Filter can be changed later when applied to a Smart Object.

title: Add your own text
steps: Choose the Horizontal Type tool.
Click where the text should begin and type your own words.
Confirm the text with the checkmark or switch tools.
why: Editable type lives on a separate text layer.

title: Edit an existing text layer
steps: Select the text layer in Layers.
Choose the Type tool and click inside existing text.
Make your own edits and confirm them.
why: Editing existing type avoids creating an accidental new text layer.

title: Change text font
steps: Select the text layer or highlight the text you want to change.
Use the font menu in the Options bar or Character panel.
Pick an available approved font and inspect readability.
why: Font changes affect the shape of characters.

title: Change text size
steps: Select the appropriate text layer or highlighted characters.
Set the font size in the Type Options bar or Character panel.
Inspect the layout and check that the title fits.
why: Font size changes type without requiring rasterization.

title: Change text color
steps: Select the text layer or highlight specific characters.
Click the text color swatch in the Type Options bar.
Choose a contrasting color and confirm.
why: Color contrast helps readers see your text against the image.

title: Text is hidden behind another layer
aliases: my text is behind the photo
steps: Locate the text layer in Layers.
Check its eye icon and move it above the covering image if appropriate.
Inspect the canvas and ensure no mask is hiding it.
why: Layer order can cover otherwise valid text.

title: Text box cuts off words
steps: Select the paragraph text with the Type tool.
Drag the text box boundary to make room.
Check all edges and confirm the edit.
why: Paragraph type wraps within its text frame.

title: Change paragraph alignment
steps: Select the text layer.
Open Window > Paragraph or use the Type Options bar.
Choose left, center or right alignment and inspect the layout.
why: Alignment positions text relative to its text origin or frame.

title: Change spacing between letters
steps: Select the text or text layer.
Open Window > Character and adjust Tracking slightly.
Inspect the word at normal size.
why: Tracking adjusts spacing across selected characters.

title: Change space between lines
steps: Select multiline text.
Open Window > Character and adjust Leading.
Check that lines no longer overlap and remain grouped visually.
why: Leading controls baseline-to-baseline line spacing.

title: Text layer will not accept brush
steps: Keep the type layer editable.
Create a separate blank layer for painting or add a layer mask where appropriate.
Return to Type tool to revise the words.
why: Type layers are not ordinary painted pixel layers.

title: Add a drop shadow to text
steps: Select the text layer and click fx in Layers.
Choose Drop Shadow and adjust opacity, distance and size gently.
Inspect readability and confirm.
why: A layer style adds an editable effect behind the type.

title: Edit an existing text stroke
steps: Expand the text layer effects in Layers.
Double-click Stroke.
Adjust size, color and position and inspect at normal zoom.
why: Stroke is an editable style, not part of the typed words.

title: Layer style is not visible
steps: Expand the layer's Effects entry.
Check the eye icon beside Effects and the individual style.
Double-click the style and inspect its size and opacity if needed.
why: Styles can exist but be hidden or too subtle to notice.

title: Create a document at required size
steps: Choose File > New.
Enter the width, height and units from your assignment directions.
Review orientation and background before creating.
why: Document dimensions set the available image area.

title: Image Size versus Canvas Size
steps: Check whether you want to scale existing pixels or change the document boundary.
Use Image > Image Size for scaling; use Image > Canvas Size for the surrounding boundary.
Save a copy before any dimension changes.
why: Image Size and Canvas Size affect different aspects of the document.

title: Crop a photo without deleting pixels
steps: Select the Crop tool and frame the area.
Uncheck Delete Cropped Pixels if available and suitable.
Confirm the crop, then save your PSD.
why: Preserving cropped pixels can allow later reframing.

title: PNG exports with transparent background
aliases: png background needs to be white
steps: Check your canvas for checkerboard areas.
Add a solid-color layer below all visible artwork if the assignment requires a background.
Export PNG and inspect the resulting file.
why: A checkerboard represents transparent pixels; an opaque background removes them.

title: Export transparent PNG
steps: Hide any unwanted background layers and check the checkerboard.
Choose File > Export > Export As, select PNG and enable Transparency if shown.
Export and reopen the PNG to check the edges.
why: PNG supports transparency; JPG does not.

title: JPG has no transparency
steps: Check whether the assignment needs transparent pixels.
Use PNG for transparency or place a solid background before saving JPG.
Inspect the exported image.
why: JPEG does not store an alpha transparency channel.

title: Exported image is too small
steps: Open the PSD and choose Export As.
Review the width, height and Scale values against assignment directions.
Export again under a clear filename and inspect the new file.
why: Export can resize output independently of the editable document.

title: Exported image missing layers
steps: Return to the original PSD and check each intended layer's visibility.
Make sure the canvas shows the full intended composition.
Export again and open the exported file to confirm.
why: Exports include the visible composition, not hidden layers.

title: Find where Photoshop saved a file
steps: Check the filename and folder shown by File > Save As or Export As without overwriting anything.
Open File Explorer and navigate to the approved folder.
Verify the extension and modified time before submitting.
why: Editable and exported files may be saved in different folders.

title: Save a second version safely
steps: Choose File > Save As and select your approved storage location.
Use a new descriptive filename while preserving PSD format.
Confirm the filename before continuing edits.
why: Versioned PSDs protect earlier work.

title: Submit PSD and exported image
steps: Save the editable PSD and export the required PNG or JPG.
Open both files to verify they are the intended version.
Attach the required files in Google Classroom following your teacher's directions.
why: The editable project and final image are different deliverables.

title: File too large to submit
steps: Keep your original layered PSD intact.
Check the assignment's file type and size requirements.
Ask your teacher whether an appropriately resized exported copy or approved Drive link is acceptable.
why: Reducing the original file may remove useful editing information.

title: Photoshop warns about saving format
steps: Read the format warning before accepting.
Save your editable work as PSD first.
Export a separate PNG or JPG if the assignment needs a flat image.
why: Not all file types preserve editable layers.

title: Missing Properties panel
steps: Open Window > Properties.
Select your object to display its relevant controls.
why: Properties changes with the selected object.

title: Missing Align panel
steps: Open Window > Align.
Select at least two objects or choose Align to Artboard for a single object.
why: The available alignment controls depend on the selection.

title: Missing Pathfinder panel
steps: Open Window > Pathfinder.
Select your own overlapping vector shapes before trying a shape mode.
why: Pathfinder acts on selected vector artwork.

title: Missing Character panel
steps: Open Window > Type > Character.
Select the text or type object to display its attributes.
why: Character controls apply to letters rather than the whole artboard.

title: Missing Stroke panel
steps: Open Window > Stroke.
Select a path and expand the panel options if needed.
why: Stroke options control the edge of a path.

title: Missing Swatches panel
steps: Open Window > Swatches.
Select your artwork and choose Fill or Stroke before picking a swatch.
why: Swatches apply to the active paint attribute.

title: Missing Gradient panel
steps: Open Window > Gradient.
Select a filled object and choose the Fill attribute.
why: The panel edits gradient colors and stops.

title: Canvas suddenly fills screen
steps: Press Esc if a presentation is active.
Press F to cycle normal Illustrator screen modes if needed, stopping when menus return.
why: Screen modes can hide the interface without losing artwork.

title: All panels vanished
steps: Press Tab once when not typing in a text field.
If panels are still absent, use Window to open the required panel.
why: Tab temporarily hides or shows many panels.

title: Only side panels vanished
steps: Press Shift + Tab once while not editing text.
Check whether the panels return and open Window for any remaining missing panel.
why: Shift + Tab toggles panels other than the toolbar and control panel.

title: Zoom out to see all artboards
steps: Choose View > Fit All in Window.
Identify the artboard with your work before selecting anything.
why: Fitting all artboards changes the view, not the design.

title: Fit one artboard in the window
steps: Select or activate the intended artboard.
Choose View > Fit Artboard in Window (Ctrl + 0).
why: Fitting a board does not resize its contents.

title: Pan around artwork
steps: Hold Space when not editing text, then drag the view.
Release Space when you reach the intended area.
why: Panning moves the view only.

title: View actual size
steps: Choose View > Actual Size or Ctrl + 1.
Use the zoom controls again if you need to see more of the board.
why: Zoom changes only the on-screen view.

title: Perspective grid will not go away
steps: Choose View > Perspective Grid > Hide Grid.
Return to the Selection tool and inspect the artwork.
why: The perspective grid is a view aid, not exported artwork.

title: Artboard edges disappeared
steps: Look under View for Show Artboards.
Choose it if available, then fit the current artboard in the window.
why: Artboard visibility affects the view only.

title: Everything else is dimmed
steps: Check for the isolation bar above the artwork.
Press Esc or use the back arrow to exit isolation mode.
why: Isolation mode limits editing to one group or object.

title: Bounding box not visible
steps: Select an object with the black Selection arrow.
Choose View > Show Bounding Box if available.
why: The bounding box provides scale and rotation handles.

title: Anchor points not visible
steps: Choose View > Show Edges if available.
Select a path with the white Direct Selection arrow.
why: Hidden edges can conceal selection points without changing paths.

title: Toolbar only has a few tools
steps: Look in Window > Toolbars for Advanced, if your teacher permits that workspace view.
Alternatively hold a related tool icon to reveal nested tools.
why: Many Illustrator tools share a toolbar slot.

title: Draw exact size rectangle
steps: Select Rectangle, then click once on the artboard.
Enter the required width and height in the dialog, and confirm.
why: Clicking instead of dragging allows precise dimensions.

title: Draw an exact circle
steps: Choose Ellipse and hold Shift while dragging.
Release the mouse before releasing Shift.
why: A modifier constrains the shape to equal width and height.

title: Round rectangle corners
steps: Select your rectangle and locate its corner widgets.
Drag a corner widget inward, or use available corner radius controls.
why: Live corner controls round the existing vector geometry.

title: Make a polygon
steps: Find Polygon under the shape tools and click the artboard.
Enter a radius and number of sides, then confirm.
why: The side count determines the regular polygon geometry.

title: Make a star
steps: Select Star and click once on the artboard.
Enter the two radii and number of points, then confirm.
why: The inner and outer radii determine how pointed a star looks.

title: Draw a straight line
steps: Select the Line Segment tool and drag between endpoints.
Hold Shift for constrained angles if needed, then assign a visible stroke.
why: An open line needs a stroke to be seen clearly.

title: Draw a grid of rectangles
steps: Find Rectangular Grid under the line tools if available.
Click the artboard and set the intended dimensions and divider counts.
why: Grid dividers produce multiple cells inside the selected area.

title: Draw concentric circles
steps: Find the Polar Grid tool under the line tools.
Click the artboard to enter size and divider counts, then add a visible stroke.
why: The polar grid makes rings and radial dividers.

title: Resize without stretching
steps: Use the Selection tool and drag a corner handle while holding Shift.
Release the mouse, then Shift; verify the shape proportions.
why: Constrained scaling preserves the aspect ratio.

title: Resize precisely with Transform
steps: Select the object and open Window > Transform.
Enter the required W or H value, using the linked proportions option if needed.
why: Transform values let you set measured dimensions.

title: Rotate to a specific angle
steps: Select your object and open Object > Transform > Rotate.
Enter the required angle, preview and confirm.
why: A numeric rotation avoids imprecise dragging.

title: Flip an object horizontally
steps: Select your object and choose Object > Transform > Reflect.
Choose the Vertical axis for a left-right mirror and preview before confirming.
why: Reflection mirrors across the chosen axis.

title: Flip an object vertically
steps: Choose Object > Transform > Reflect for the selected object.
Choose the Horizontal axis to flip top to bottom; preview and confirm.
why: The axis is the mirror line, not the direction of movement.

title: Duplicate with Alt drag
steps: Select your own object with the black arrow.
Hold Alt while dragging to create a copy, then release the mouse.
why: Alt-drag duplicates instead of moving the original.

title: Repeat the last transform
steps: Create a copy with the required move or rotation.
Choose Object > Transform > Transform Again (Ctrl + D) to repeat it.
why: Illustrator remembers the most recent transform operation.

title: Move by an exact amount
steps: Select the object and choose Object > Transform > Move.
Enter horizontal and vertical distances and preview; choose OK or Copy as intended.
why: Precise moves help keep layouts consistent.

title: Paste in front
steps: Copy your selected object with Ctrl + C.
Use Edit > Paste in Front to put a duplicate directly in front of the copied selection.
why: The copy starts at the same position, so it can look like nothing changed.

title: Paste behind
steps: Copy the selected object.
Choose Edit > Paste in Back and inspect the Layers panel if the copy is covered.
why: Stack order determines what is visible.

title: Scale stroke separately from shape
steps: Select the object and open Object > Transform > Scale.
Review Scale Strokes & Effects in the dialog, choose the intended behavior, and preview.
why: Scaling geometry and scaling stroke weights are separate choices.

title: Object moves too far with arrow keys
steps: Select the object with the black arrow.
Use the Transform panel X and Y values for precise placement rather than changing global preferences.
why: Document coordinates permit exact adjustments without system changes.

title: Black arrow versus white arrow
steps: Use the black Selection tool for whole objects.
Use the white Direct Selection tool for anchor points or path segments.
why: The two tools select different levels of vector geometry.

title: Draw angular path with Pen
steps: Select Pen and click a starting point.
Click additional corners; click the start again to close, or press Esc to end an open path.
why: Individual clicks create corner anchors.

title: Draw curves with Pen
steps: Select Pen and click-drag to establish direction handles.
Click-drag the next anchor to shape the curve; adjust with Direct Selection afterward.
why: Handles control the direction and curvature of adjoining segments.

title: Curvature tool basics
steps: Select Curvature and click successive points along the intended curve.
Double-click a point when a corner is needed; finish the path as appropriate.
why: The tool calculates smooth curves between points.

title: Stop drawing with Pen
steps: Press Esc to finish the current open path.
Select the black arrow before moving other artwork.
why: Ending a path prevents the next click from extending it.

title: Close an open path
steps: With the Pen tool, continue from an endpoint of your own path.
Click the original endpoint when the close-path cursor appears.
why: A closed path encloses an area for fill and shape operations.

title: Join two endpoints
steps: Use Direct Selection to select the two intended open endpoints.
Choose Object > Path > Join (Ctrl + J).
why: Joining connects the selected path ends.

title: Average two endpoints first
steps: Select the intended endpoints with Direct Selection.
Choose Object > Path > Average, select Both if appropriate, then confirm; join if needed.
why: Averaging moves points to a shared position before joining.

title: Add an anchor point
steps: Select your path and choose Add Anchor Point under the Pen tool.
Click a point along the existing path, then edit it with Direct Selection.
why: Adding an anchor provides another location to control geometry.

title: Remove an extra anchor
steps: Select the Delete Anchor Point tool under Pen.
Click an unnecessary anchor on your own path; undo if the shape changes undesirably.
why: Removing an anchor with this tool preserves path continuity.

title: Convert corner to smooth
steps: Choose Anchor Point tool and drag from the chosen corner anchor.
Adjust the resulting handles with Direct Selection.
why: A smooth point has handles that shape curves on both sides.

title: Convert smooth point to corner
steps: Choose Anchor Point tool and click the intended smooth anchor.
Check the shape and undo if necessary.
why: Corner points allow abrupt direction changes.

title: Move one anchor point
steps: Choose Direct Selection and click the desired anchor.
Drag only that selected point, or use arrows to nudge it.
why: Direct Selection changes the path without moving the whole object.

title: Cut a path at two points
steps: Select Scissors and click the intended anchor or segment locations.
Select and move one resulting segment to verify it; undo if needed.
why: Scissors splits paths rather than trimming by a filled area.

title: Slice a filled shape
steps: Save a copy or duplicate your own shape first.
Choose Knife, drag a cut across the shape, then select the resulting pieces.
why: Knife can divide a filled vector object into separate shapes.

title: Erase part of vector artwork
steps: Select only the object you intend to edit.
Drag the Eraser over a small test area and check the resulting paths.
why: Selection restricts which editable objects are affected.

title: Smooth a rough path
steps: Duplicate your original path for safety.
Select Smooth and drag along the rough segment; compare the result.
why: Smoothing reduces irregular path geometry.

title: Simplify dense vector points
steps: Duplicate the artwork, then select the copy.
Choose Object > Path > Simplify and preview before accepting.
why: Simplification reduces anchors and can change fine detail.

title: Find and remove stray points
steps: Inspect the document in Outline view if needed.
Use Select > Object > Stray Points if available, examine the selected points, and delete only unwanted points of your own work.
why: Unconnected points can be left behind by editing.

title: Offset a path
steps: Select your shape and choose Object > Path > Offset Path.
Enter an offset, preview the new path, and confirm if correct.
why: An offset creates a new contour at a measured distance.

title: Remove the fill only
steps: Select the object and activate Fill in the toolbar.
Choose the None swatch, leaving Stroke visible if wanted.
why: Removing fill makes the interior unpainted.

title: Remove the stroke only
steps: Select the object and activate Stroke.
Choose None, leaving the fill unchanged.
why: Fill and stroke can be edited independently.

title: Swap fill and stroke
steps: Select the object and use the small swap arrow near Fill and Stroke.
Check the result and undo if needed.
why: The swap exchanges both paint attributes.

title: Reset default paint colors
steps: Select your own object and press D while not editing text.
Check the default white fill and black stroke; undo if undesired.
why: D applies the standard paint attributes.

title: Outline has wrong thickness
steps: Select the object and open Stroke or Properties.
Enter the desired stroke weight and inspect at normal zoom.
why: Weight sets the thickness of the path outline.

title: Make dashed lines
steps: Select a stroked path and open Window > Stroke.
Enable Dashed Line and enter dash and gap values.
why: Dash settings create repeated painted and unpainted segments.

title: Round line ends
steps: Select the open stroked path and open Stroke.
Choose Round Cap and compare the end appearance.
why: Caps affect the endpoints of open strokes.

title: Round stroke corners
steps: Select the stroked object and choose Round Join in Stroke.
Inspect the corners and compare with the original.
why: Joins determine how stroke edges meet at corners.

title: Align stroke inside shape
steps: Select a closed vector path and open Stroke.
Choose Align Stroke to Inside if available; compare the outline.
why: Stroke alignment positions the outline relative to the path.

title: Sample color from another object
steps: Select the object that should receive the appearance.
Choose Eyedropper and click the source artwork; undo if extra appearance attributes were copied.
why: Eyedropper can sample appearance as well as color.

title: Enter a hex color
steps: Select your object and double-click the active Fill or Stroke swatch.
Enter the required hex value if the color picker offers it, then confirm.
why: Numeric color values support consistent palettes.

title: Save reusable color swatch
steps: Choose the desired color, then open Window > Swatches.
Use New Swatch and name it clearly.
why: Swatches let you reuse colors throughout the document.

title: Change one gradient stop
steps: Select the object and open Gradient.
Double-click the desired color stop and select its new color.
why: Each stop controls color at a different gradient position.

title: Change gradient direction
steps: Select the gradient-filled object.
Use Gradient tool to drag the direction, or enter an available angle in Gradient.
why: Gradient direction controls the transition across the shape.

title: Make a radial gradient
steps: Select your filled shape and open Gradient.
Choose Radial and adjust the stops and position as needed.
why: A radial gradient spreads from a center point.

title: Add a gradient color stop
steps: Select the gradient object and open Gradient.
Click beneath the gradient slider to add a stop, then assign its color.
why: Additional stops introduce intermediate colors.

title: Remove an unwanted gradient stop
steps: Select the stop in Gradient.
Drag it away from the slider or use the delete stop control if available.
why: Removing a stop simplifies the transition.

title: Set object opacity
steps: Select the object and open Properties or Window > Transparency.
Adjust opacity and preview against other objects.
why: Opacity changes how much underlying artwork shows through.

title: Make a variable-width stroke
steps: Select a stroked path and choose Width tool.
Drag outward on a point of the stroke to change local width.
why: Width points vary stroke thickness along a path.

title: Artwork color looks faded
steps: Select the object and inspect opacity in Transparency.
Check Appearance for unexpected effects; compare with other objects and restore only unintended changes.
why: Opacity and appearance effects can alter visible color.

title: Add a drop shadow
steps: Select your object and open Effect > Stylize > Drop Shadow (Illustrator effects).
Preview modest opacity, offset and blur, then confirm or cancel.
why: A live effect adds a shadow without changing the original path.

title: Edit a live effect
steps: Select the object and open Window > Appearance.
Click the effect name to reopen its dialog, then preview the change.
why: Live effects stay editable in Appearance.

title: Remove a live effect
steps: Select the object and open Appearance.
Select the intended effect entry and use its delete control, not the object itself.
why: Removing the effect preserves the underlying geometry.

title: Add another stroke
steps: Select the object and open Appearance.
Use Add New Stroke and set its weight and color; rearrange appearance order if needed.
why: Appearance can stack multiple strokes on one object.

title: Subtract with Shape Builder
steps: Select your intended overlapping vector shapes and choose Shape Builder.
Hold Alt and click or drag across the unwanted regions; review and undo mistakes.
why: Alt switches the tool from combining to subtracting.

title: Shape Builder does nothing
steps: Select the editable vector paths together with the Selection tool.
Check that the regions meet or overlap and try Shape Builder on a small region.
why: The tool needs eligible selected paths and usable regions.

title: Shape Builder leaves small gaps
steps: Zoom in and inspect the actual endpoints and intersections.
Adjust your own anchors so the intended regions meet, then retry.
why: Visible outlines may appear connected while the underlying paths are separated.

title: Unite overlapping objects
steps: Duplicate your original shapes if you may need them later.
Select the overlapping shapes and choose Unite in Window > Pathfinder.
why: Unite combines filled regions into a single resulting shape or compound path.

title: Cut front shape out of back
steps: Arrange the cutter above the base object and select both.
Choose Minus Front in Pathfinder; undo if the wrong object disappears.
why: Minus Front subtracts front shapes from the back shape.

title: Keep only overlap
steps: Select your overlapping vector shapes.
Choose Intersect in Pathfinder and inspect the remaining area.
why: Intersect retains their common area.

title: Remove overlap but keep outer pieces
steps: Select the two overlapping vector shapes.
Choose Exclude in Pathfinder and inspect the resulting shape.
why: Exclude removes the shared region between two overlapping shapes.

title: Split every overlapping region
steps: Duplicate originals and select the intended overlapping shapes.
Choose Divide in Pathfinder, then ungroup or directly select the resulting regions.
why: Divide separates artwork at intersections.

title: Pathfinder removes wrong shape
steps: Undo the last operation.
Inspect stacking order in Layers; put the cutter on top before trying Minus Front again.
why: Subtraction depends on which object is in front.

title: Make a hole inside a shape
steps: Put a smaller closed shape inside a larger closed shape and select both.
Choose Object > Compound Path > Make and inspect the hole.
why: Compound paths can define unpainted interiors.

title: Release a compound path
steps: Select the compound path and save a copy if needed.
Choose Object > Compound Path > Release, then inspect fill and order of the separate paths.
why: Release returns constituent paths, which may have different visible appearance.

title: Crop artwork with a shape
steps: Place a closed vector shape above the artwork to be cropped.
Select both, then choose Object > Clipping Mask > Make.
why: The upper path defines what remains visible without deleting hidden areas.

title: Clipping mask is blank
steps: Undo and ensure the intended vector clipping path is above the artwork.
Select both the path and the artwork, then make the mask again.
why: The topmost selected object becomes the clipping path.

title: Move image inside clipping mask
steps: Select the clipped group and use Direct Selection to select its contents or enter isolation mode.
Move the image, not the clipping path; exit isolation and check the crop.
why: Mask geometry and its contents remain separately editable.

title: Change clipping mask shape
steps: Select the clipping group and locate its clipping path in Layers.
Edit the path using Direct Selection or choose Object > Clipping Mask > Edit Mask.
why: A mask can be edited without replacing the image.

title: Uncrop a clipping mask
steps: Select the clipping group.
Choose Object > Clipping Mask > Release, then inspect the formerly hidden contents.
why: Releasing makes the original artwork visible again.

title: Draw inside existing shape
steps: Select one suitable closed shape and choose Draw Inside at the bottom of the toolbar.
Draw the intended artwork and return to Draw Normal afterward.
why: Draw Inside clips new marks to the chosen shape.

title: Drawing goes behind everything
steps: Check the drawing mode at the bottom of the toolbar.
Choose Draw Normal before creating another object.
why: Draw Behind inserts artwork beneath the selected object or existing stack.

title: Live Paint Bucket basics
steps: Select your artwork and choose Object > Live Paint > Make.
Use Live Paint Bucket to fill the intended faces with your selected color.
why: Live Paint treats bounded regions as individually paintable areas.

title: Live Paint refuses to fill region
steps: Check that the artwork is a Live Paint group.
Inspect open gaps at normal zoom; correct your own paths or use approved Live Paint gap controls.
why: A gap can prevent a region from being recognized as closed.

title: Expand Live Paint artwork
steps: Save an editable copy before expanding.
Select the Live Paint group and choose Object > Live Paint > Expand; inspect the resulting objects.
why: Expansion converts live regions into ordinary editable vector objects.

title: Convert stroke to a filled shape
steps: Duplicate the stroked path if needed for future edits.
Choose Object > Path > Outline Stroke on the copy.
why: An outlined stroke becomes filled vector geometry rather than a stroke attribute.

title: Expand appearance safely
steps: Save a copy of the original artwork.
Select the live-effect object and choose Object > Expand Appearance if available.
why: Expansion may create more paths and remove live-effect editability.

title: Text cursor will not leave typing
steps: Press Esc to exit text editing.
Choose the black Selection arrow and click the type object.
why: Text editing and object selection are separate modes.

title: Change font family
steps: Select your text or the whole type object.
Choose a teacher-approved installed font in Character or Properties.
why: A selected font changes the appearance of your own words.

title: Change font size
steps: Select the intended text or type object.
Set its font size in Character or Properties.
why: Font size controls letter scale without needing to drag the entire object.

title: Change text color
steps: Select the intended characters or the type object.
Activate Fill and choose a color; avoid changing the stroke accidentally.
why: Type inherits fill and stroke like other vector artwork.

title: Bold or italic text
steps: Select your text and open Character.
Choose an available Bold or Italic font style if that family includes it.
why: Font styles depend on the installed font family.

title: Create a paragraph text box
steps: Select Type and drag a rectangle on the artboard.
Enter your own text and resize the area with Selection if needed.
why: Area type wraps text inside a defined boundary.

title: Text box has red plus
steps: Select the area type object and find its overflow indicator.
Enlarge the text area or use a suitable smaller font size; check that all words appear.
why: The plus indicates more text than fits inside the box.

title: Convert point type to area type
steps: Select your point type object.
Choose Type > Convert to Area Type if available, then resize its text area.
why: Area type flows within a defined boundary.

title: Point type stretched accidentally
steps: Undo the unwanted transform.
Adjust size using Character and preserve proportions with the Selection tool.
why: Changing font size is different from distorting the object.

title: Adjust space between lines
steps: Select the text and open Character.
Change Leading and check the visual spacing.
why: Leading controls the distance between text baselines.

title: Change spacing across a word
steps: Select the intended word or text range.
Adjust Tracking in Character and inspect readability.
why: Tracking adds or removes spacing across multiple selected characters.

title: Adjust spacing between two letters
steps: Place the text cursor between the two letters.
Adjust Kerning in Character and compare the pair.
why: Kerning controls spacing for an individual letter pair.

title: Align a paragraph
steps: Select your type object or put the cursor in the paragraph.
Open Window > Type > Paragraph and choose left, center, or right alignment.
why: Paragraph alignment positions lines within the text area or relative to its point.

title: Make superscript characters
steps: Select the specific characters in your text.
Use Superscript in Character panel options if available.
why: Superscript raises and typically reduces selected characters.

title: Make subscript characters
steps: Select the intended characters.
Choose Subscript from the Character panel options if available.
why: Subscript positions characters below the main baseline.

title: Move selected letters up or down
steps: Select only the desired characters.
Set Baseline Shift in Character and compare with neighboring letters.
why: Baseline shift adjusts vertical placement without moving the entire text object.

title: Put text around a circle
steps: Draw a circle and keep a separate colored copy if needed.
Choose Type on a Path and click the circle edge; enter your own words.
why: Type follows the selected path, whose original paint may be removed.

title: Text on path is upside down
steps: Select the type-on-path object.
Use Type > Type on a Path > Type on a Path Options and check Flip, or drag the center bracket across the path.
why: The flip option changes which side of the path carries text.

title: Move text along a curve
steps: Select the type-on-path object and locate its brackets.
Drag the center bracket along the path without crossing it unless intentionally flipping.
why: The brackets define the position of the type along its path.

title: Text on path disappears
steps: Select the path type and inspect the start and end brackets.
Move the brackets to allow more room or reduce the font size.
why: Type requires enough usable path length for all characters.

title: Warp text with live effect
steps: Select your type object and save an editable copy if needed.
Choose Effect > Warp and preview an appropriate style; adjust the bend.
why: A live warp changes appearance while preserving editable type.

title: Convert text to outlines
steps: Keep a copy of the original live text.
Select the duplicate and choose Type > Create Outlines.
why: Outlined letters become vector paths and no longer edit as ordinary text.

title: Cannot type into outlined letters
steps: Check whether Type tool produces a text cursor in the existing lettering.
If the letters are paths, locate your saved live-text copy or recreate your own text.
why: Outlining removes live type information.

title: Missing font warning
steps: Read the missing-font list and keep the original file intact.
Select a teacher-approved installed substitute if directed; do not install fonts on school computers.
why: Font availability varies between computers.

title: Outline a title with a stroke
steps: Select the text object and open Appearance.
Add or adjust a Stroke entry and choose a legible weight; move the stroke beneath the fill in Appearance if needed.
why: A stroke below the fill keeps the letter interiors readable.

title: Insert a special character
steps: Place the Type cursor where you need the symbol.
Open Window > Type > Glyphs and double-click an available glyph.
why: Glyphs are characters included in the selected font.

title: Text behind other artwork
steps: Find the type object in Layers and select it.
Adjust its stacking with Object > Arrange or move the layer within your own artwork.
why: Other objects can cover otherwise valid text.

title: Center object on artboard
steps: Select your object and open Align.
Set Align To to Artboard; choose Horizontal Align Center and Vertical Align Center.
why: The artboard becomes the alignment reference.

title: Align several objects to each other
steps: Select the intended objects and open Align.
Set Align To Selection and choose matching edge or center alignment.
why: The selected set provides the alignment boundary.

title: Align to a key object
steps: Select the objects, then click the desired reference object again without holding Shift.
Confirm the highlighted key object and apply the intended alignment.
why: The key object stays fixed while others align to it.

title: Space objects evenly
steps: Select at least three intended objects and open Align.
Choose the appropriate Distribute Spacing control; use key-object alignment for a fixed gap if needed.
why: Equal gaps differ from equal center-to-center distances.

title: Show document grid
steps: Choose View > Show Grid.
Use View > Hide Grid when finished.
why: The document grid is a view aid and does not appear in exported artwork.

title: Objects keep snapping to grid
steps: Check View > Snap to Grid in your own document.
Turn that view option off if the assignment permits, then position the object.
why: Snapping can constrain a drag to nearby grid positions.

title: Smart Guides missing
steps: Check View > Smart Guides and enable it if appropriate.
Drag a selected object near another edge and watch for guide hints.
why: Smart Guides provide temporary alignment hints while editing.

title: Show rulers
steps: Choose View > Rulers > Show Rulers.
Use the displayed rulers to check placement on the artboard.
why: Rulers show document measurements without printing them.

title: Make a ruler guide
steps: Show rulers using View > Rulers > Show Rulers.
Drag from a ruler onto the artboard to create a guide.
why: Guides help position artwork and do not export as design objects.

title: Guide will not move
steps: Check View > Guides > Lock Guides.
Only if these are your own guides and the teacher permits, unlock guides, adjust the intended guide, and relock as needed.
why: Guide locking prevents accidental layout changes.

title: Hide guide lines
steps: Choose View > Guides > Hide Guides.
Check the exported image if you are unsure whether lines were guides or actual paths.
why: Guides are nonprinting layout aids; real paths remain visible.

title: Create an extra artboard
steps: Select the Artboard tool (Shift + O).
Drag a new artboard in an empty workspace area or use New Artboard in Artboards.
why: Multiple artboards allow separate designs in one document.

title: Rename an artboard
steps: Open Window > Artboards.
Double-click or open the options for the intended artboard and enter its name.
why: Names help identify boards and may become export filenames.

title: Reorder artboards
steps: Open Window > Artboards and select the intended board.
Use the panel's reorder controls, then verify the listed order.
why: Document order can differ from the physical layout on screen.

title: Move artboard with its artwork
steps: Select the Artboard tool and locate the board.
Enable Move Artwork with Artboard if available before dragging; inspect the result and undo if it moves unintended work.
why: Artboard movement can optionally carry its artwork.

title: Resize artboard without changing artwork
steps: Select Artboard tool and the intended board.
Set its width and height or drag its boundary; verify artwork has not been scaled.
why: Artboards define output regions independently of object size.

title: Landscape versus portrait artboard
steps: Select the correct artboard with Artboard tool.
Choose the desired orientation or enter swapped W and H values.
why: Orientation changes the board boundary, not necessarily the artwork direction.

title: Remove an extra artboard safely
steps: Open Artboards and identify the unwanted board; preserve your work.
Remove only the unwanted board, then inspect leftover artwork and the remaining board order.
why: Deleting an artboard does not automatically delete its artwork.

title: Preview just the artboard
steps: Choose View > Trim View if available.
Switch back to normal view when you need to edit off-board objects.
why: Trim View previews cropped artwork without deleting outside geometry.

title: Arrange repeated rows
steps: Create one approved object and duplicate it at a measured offset.
Use Transform Again or Align distribution to repeat and space the row; duplicate the row for additional rows.
why: Measured duplication and distribution produce consistent spacing.

title: Set up a bleed for print
steps: Check whether your teacher actually requires bleed and ask for the amount.
Use File > Document Setup to inspect document bleed and extend background artwork only as directed.
why: Bleed is a print allowance outside the trim boundary.

title: Make a new layer
steps: Open Window > Layers and select the intended location.
Click Create New Layer and rename it before adding artwork.
why: Independent layers organize objects and stacking.

title: Rename a layer
steps: Open the Layers panel and identify your own layer.
Double-click its name or open Layer Options and enter a meaningful label.
why: Clear names make objects easier to locate.

title: Hide a layer temporarily
steps: Locate your own layer in Layers.
Click its visibility eye, then restore it before saving or exporting if required.
why: Hiding a layer does not erase its contents.

title: Lock a background layer
steps: Find the background layer in Layers.
Click its lock column to protect it while editing other layers.
why: Locking prevents accidental selection and edits.

title: Unlock your own object
steps: Locate the object or layer and its lock in Layers.
Unlock only your own accidentally locked artwork, not any teacher-protected items.
why: A lock blocks selection and editing until released.

title: Move artwork to another layer
steps: Select the intended object and open Layers.
Drag its colored selection indicator to the correct unlocked layer and check stacking.
why: Moving the selection indicator relocates the object without recreating it.

title: Group related objects
steps: Select the related objects with Selection and Shift-click.
Choose Object > Group (Ctrl + G).
why: Grouping allows multiple objects to move as one unit.

title: Ungroup artwork
steps: Select your own group.
Choose Object > Ungroup (Ctrl + Shift + G) and check which objects can now be selected individually.
why: Ungroup removes one level of grouping at a time.

title: Edit inside a group
steps: Double-click the intended group with Selection.
Edit only the desired child object and press Esc to leave isolation.
why: Isolation temporarily limits selections to the group.

title: Select hidden object in Layers
steps: Expand the relevant layer or group in Layers.
Use the selection column at the right of the desired item to select it, then inspect the highlight.
why: Layers can locate artwork that is difficult to click directly.

title: Send object behind others
steps: Select your intended object.
Use Object > Arrange > Send to Back or Send Backward, depending on how far it should move.
why: Arrange affects relative stacking within the active hierarchy.

title: Place an image file
steps: Choose File > Place and select the teacher-approved image file.
Click or drag on the intended artboard and check its size.
why: Placed images can remain linked or be embedded in the document.

title: Missing linked image warning
steps: Open Window > Links and locate the missing file entry.
Use Relink to choose the correct approved original file; ask the teacher if you cannot locate it.
why: Linked artwork depends on an accessible external file.

title: Embed a linked image
steps: Select the placed image and open Links or Properties.
Choose Embed or Embed Image if available; save a copy if appropriate.
why: Embedding stores image data with the AI document but can increase file size.

title: Image looks pixelated in Illustrator
steps: Select the placed photo and inspect it at 100 percent zoom.
Use a higher-resolution approved original rather than stretching a small image excessively.
why: Raster photographs retain their pixel limits even in a vector document.

title: Image Trace basics
steps: Use a teacher-approved source image and keep the original.
Select it, open Window > Image Trace, and preview a suitable preset; expand a copy only if editable paths are needed.
why: Image Trace approximates raster shapes with vector paths; it is not image generation.

title: Image Trace has too much detail
steps: Select the live trace and open Image Trace.
Preview a simpler preset or fewer colors and compare the result before expanding.
why: Trace complexity affects detail and the number of paths.

title: Export only one artboard
steps: Save the AI first and choose File > Export > Export As.
Enable Use Artboards and enter the intended board range; select the required format and inspect output.
why: A range limits export to specified artboards.

title: Export every artboard at once
steps: Choose File > Export > Export for Screens and select the Artboards tab.
Select the required boards, output folder and format; export and inspect each file.
why: Batch export creates separate outputs for multiple boards.

title: PNG has a white background
steps: Check for a real white shape behind the artwork and hide only your own unwanted background.
Export PNG with Transparent background if the dialog offers it; reopen the output.
why: PNG can store transparent pixels, but actual white artwork remains white.

title: PNG should have a colored background
steps: Create a rectangle that covers the artboard and place it behind your artwork.
Assign the required fill and export with Use Artboards; check the resulting PNG.
why: A solid object supplies a planned background color.

title: Exported image includes extra artwork
steps: Open Export As from the saved AI document.
Enable Use Artboards and choose the intended range; verify the new file.
why: Use Artboards restricts export to board boundaries.

title: Exported image looks blurry
steps: Check the requested output size and open the original AI.
Export again using appropriate resolution or scale for the assignment; inspect the new file at normal size.
why: Raster export quality depends on its pixel dimensions.

title: Export SVG for vector use
steps: Keep the original editable AI file.
Choose File > Export > Export As and select SVG; use the teacher-required options and inspect the result.
why: SVG represents scalable artwork but may handle effects and fonts differently.

title: Save PDF copy
steps: Save the editable AI first.
Choose File > Save a Copy or Save As and select Adobe PDF; use the requested options.
why: PDF is useful for viewing and printing but should not replace the working AI.

title: Find exported files
steps: Check the destination folder in the export dialog without overwriting anything.
Open File Explorer and compare filenames and modified times in that folder.
why: The export destination may differ from the working document folder.

title: Submit AI and PNG together
steps: Save the editable AI, then export the required image.
Open each to verify it, and attach both in Classroom according to assignment directions.
why: The teacher may need both editable geometry and the finished image.

title: Keep an earlier version
steps: Choose File > Save As and use a new descriptive filename in your approved folder.
Verify you are working on the intended copy before further edits.
why: Versioned copies preserve earlier stages of a design.

title: AI file not opening from browser
steps: Check that you downloaded the correct AI file to the approved location.
Open it through Illustrator rather than relying on a browser preview; ask a teacher if it still cannot open.
why: Browser previews may not support native Illustrator artwork.

title: Export warning about missing fonts
steps: Keep the original live-text AI and read the warning.
Ask whether a copy with outlined text or an approved font is acceptable; verify the export.
why: Different machines and formats can render unavailable fonts differently.

title: Illustrator freezes during export
steps: Wait briefly for complex artwork to finish and avoid repeated clicks.
If it remains frozen, tell your teacher before closing the app; do not use administrative tools.
why: Forced closure can lose unsaved work.

title: Adobe file save fails
steps: Check the filename and use an approved writable school folder.
If Save As to a new name fails, leave the document open and ask your teacher.
why: Saving to an unavailable location can fail even when artwork is intact.

title: Screenshot Illustrator progress
steps: Show the artwork and relevant tool or Layers panel on screen.
Use Windows + Shift + S to capture the required area, then save or paste it as your teacher directs.
why: Progress screenshots document the tools and steps you used.
